Hankel determinants of weighted binary sums of digitsThanks: The research of the authors was supported by a grant of the National Science Centre (NCN), Poland, no. UMO-2019/34/E/ST1/00094

Bartosz Sobolewski and Maciej Ulas
Abstract.

Let s𝐰s_{\mathbf{w}} be the weighted binary sum-of-digits function associated with an arbitrary sequence of complex weights 𝐰=(wj)j≥0\mathbf{w}=(w_{j})_{j\geq 0}. We investigate Hankel determinants ℋ𝐰​(n)=det[s𝐰​(i+j)]0≤i,j<n\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)=\det[s_{\mathbf{w}}(i+j)]_{0\leq i,j<n} and derive a general recursion that allows us to effectively compute ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) for all nn. Applying it to the ordinary binary sum-of-digits, that is, wj=1w_{j}=1, we express ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) in a closed form for several sequences of indices, including the remarkably simple

ℋ𝐰​(⌈2k+2/3⌉)=(−1)(k+2)​(k+3)2​(k+1).\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(\lceil 2^{k+2}/3\rceil)=(-1)^{\frac{(k+2)(k+3)}{2}}(k+1).

This yields an infinite family of explicit evaluations, giving a partial solution to a problem posed by Allouche and Shallit. Moreover, we closely study the specialization wj=tjw_{j}=t^{j}, where the determinants become polynomials in tt, and investigate their vanishing. For t=2​ζt=2\zeta, where ζ\zeta is a root of unity, we show that the determinants vanish on a large structured set of indices, while the complementary is sparse but infinite.

In addition to ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n), we consider Hankel determinants associated with the first difference of s𝐰s_{\mathbf{w}}, obtaining an explicit product formula. This generalizes the results by Fokkink, Kraaikamp, and Shallit concerning Hankel determinants for the period-doubling sequence.

Key words and phrases: 
sum of digits function, Hankel determinant, root of unity
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11B85; Secondary 05A15, 11B83, 15B05

1. Introduction

By the nnth Hankel matrix of a sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0}, we mean a matrix of the form

H⁡(n)=[ai+j]0≤i,j<n.H(n)=\bigl[a_{i+j}\bigr]_{0\leq i,j<n}.

Hankel matrices and the corresponding Hankel determinants detH⁡(n)\det H(n) occur naturally in several classical contexts, including moment problems, continued fractions, Padé approximation, orthogonal polynomials, automata theory, and Diophantine approximation. For instance, a real sequence (an)n≥0(a_{n})_{n\geq 0} is the moment sequence of a positive Borel measure μ\mu on the real line if and only if all Hankel matrices are positive semi-definite. This is a solution of the classical Hamburger moment problem on the real line. Moreover, Hankel determinants control the existence and norms of the associated monic orthogonal polynomials. Thus, in this classical setting, the sequence of Hankel determinants encodes important structural information about the underlying moment sequence. Another application of Hankel determinants was developed by Bugeaud, Han, Wen, and Yao [4], who used them as an effective method in the study of irrationality exponents of automatic and related numbers. Their approach uses Padé approximants constructed from generating functions, with the non-vanishing of suitable Hankel determinants guaranteeing approximants of the required order. In this way, Hankel determinants connect the combinatorial structure of automatic sequences with sharp Diophantine approximation results, including cases where direct control of the continued fraction expansion is unavailable.

In the present paper, we pursue the line of research concerning the evaluation of Hankel determinants associated with digital and automatic sequences, which was initiated by the work of Allouche, Peyrière, Wen and Wen [1]. They proved non-vanishing of Hankel determinants associated with the Thue–Morse sequence, as well as the 22-automaticity of a related two-dimensional sequence of determinants (reduced modulo 22). The former result was later proved using combinatorial methods by Bugeaud and Han [3], while the latter was extended by Guo and Wen [9] to kkth order differences of the Thue–Morse sequence.

Han [6] developed “Hankel determinant calculus”, which supplies explicit evaluation techniques (modulo a suitable integer) for several classes of automatic and Thue–Morse-like sequences, and later introduced the notion of Hankel continued fractions [7]. The latter work connects the sequence of Hankel determinants of a formal power series with specific continued fraction expansions and yields, in many situations, periodicity and algebraic descriptions of the associated determinants. These methods have become useful tools for handling Hankel determinants of sequences satisfying self-similar functional equations or substitution rules. Another important structural result was obtained by Hu and Han [8], who proved that for a large class of ±1\pm 1-valued automatic sequences defined through infinite product representations, the Hankel determinant sequence reduced modulo 22 is itself automatic. Thus, despite the complexity of computing the exact values of Hankel determinants, the resulting sequence retains the underlying regularity of the original automatic sequence. This phenomenon supports the viewpoint that Hankel determinants often reflect the intrinsic automaton-theoretic structure. Beyond the setting of automatic sequences, we note that the classical determinant calculus developed by Krattenthaler [10, 11] is a valuable computational tool.

Exact evaluations of the determinants detH⁡(n)\det H(n) are rare in this area, as most results focus on their behavior modulo an integer. A notable exception is the work of Fokkink, Kraaikamp, and Shallit [5]. They computed closed expressions for the Hankel determinants of the period-doubling sequence, revealing a link to Jacobsthal numbers and obtaining the precise recursive structure underlying the determinants.

1.1. The present work

The fundamental goal of the present study is to proceed in this direction of exactly evaluating Hankel determinants for digital sequences. Our starting point is the following problem found in the monograph by Allouche and Shallit [2, p. 208, Problem 4] (worded slightly differently).

Problem 1.1.

Find a simple closed form for the determinants of Hankel matrices given by H⁡(n)=[s⁡(i+j)]0≤i,j<nH(n)=[s(i+j)]_{0\leq i,j<n}, where ss is the binary sum of digits function.

The sequence (detH⁡(n))n≥1(\det H(n))_{n\geq 1} is A056886 in the OEIS [15] and begins with

0,−1,2,5,−8,3,8,141,−204,11,−4,−11,−30,99,1836,164997,….0,-1,2,5,-8,3,8,141,-204,11,-4,-11,-30,99,1836,164997,\ldots.

A natural approach here is to establish a recursion involving detH⁡(n)\det H(n), using the self-similarity of the sum-of-digits function. However, when performing matrix operations to reduce the size of the determinant, it becomes apparent that the contribution of digits at certain positions may be perturbed. Therefore, working with just the ordinary sum of digits becomes too restrictive, and it is (more or less) necessary to extend the scope to a more general family of functions, namely weighted binary sums of digits. More precisely, let 𝐰=(wj)j≥0\mathbf{w}=(w_{j})_{j\geq 0} be a sequence of complex weights. Then for a number n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} with binary expansion n=2l​εl+⋯+2​ε1+ε0n=2^{l}\varepsilon_{l}+\cdots+2\varepsilon_{1}+\varepsilon_{0}, where εi∈{0,1}\varepsilon_{i}\in\{0,1\}, its weighted binary sum of digits s𝐰​(n)s_{\mathbf{w}}(n) is defined by

s𝐰​(n):=wl​εl+⋯+w1​ε1+w0​ε0.s_{\mathbf{w}}(n):=w_{l}\varepsilon_{l}+\cdots+w_{1}\varepsilon_{1}+w_{0}\varepsilon_{0}.

In particular, if all weights are equal to 11, then s𝐰s_{\mathbf{w}} is the usual binary sum-of-digits function. For n≥1n\geq 1 we define the associated Hankel matrices

H𝐰​(n):=[s𝐰​(i+j)]0≤i,j<nH_{\mathbf{w}}(n):=[s_{\mathbf{w}}(i+j)]_{0\leq i,j<n}

and determinants

ℋ𝐰​(n):=detH𝐰​(n).\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n):=\det H_{\mathbf{w}}(n).

The central result of this paper (Theorem 4.2) establishes a set of recursive formulas that allow us to effectively calculate exact values of ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) for all nn. This already provides a partial solution to Problem 1.1 in a more general setting. We explore various consequences of this theorem, ranging from a general structural description of the determinants ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) to a detailed analysis of their behavior for special weights and indices.

Although we do not obtain a single closed form for arbitrary nn, in the case of the ordinary sum-of-digits function we can explicitly evaluate detH⁡(n)\det H(n) for several infinite families of indices such as n=nk:=⌈2k+2/3⌉n=n_{k}:=\lceil 2^{k+2}/3\rceil, n=2kn=2^{k}, and n=2k±1n=2^{k}\pm 1. Most interestingly, in the first case a particularly simple formula holds:

(1) detH⁡(nk)=(−1)(k+2)​(k+3)2​(k+1).\det H(n_{k})=(-1)^{\frac{(k+2)(k+3)}{2}}(k+1).

The behavior of ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) for polynomial weights wj=tjw_{j}=t^{j} turns out to be quite interesting as well. To distinguish this case from the generic one, for n=2l​εl+⋯+2​ε1+ε0n=2^{l}\varepsilon_{l}+\cdots+2\varepsilon_{1}+\varepsilon_{0} instead of s𝐰​(n)s_{\mathbf{w}}(n) we write S⁡(n,t)S(n,t), that is,

S⁡(n,t):=∑j=0lεj​tj.S(n,t):=\sum_{j=0}^{l}\varepsilon_{j}t^{j}.

We use the following special notation for related Hankel matrices and determinants:

H⁡(n,t)\displaystyle H(n,t) :=[S⁡(i+j,t)]0≤i,j<n,\displaystyle:=[S(i+j,t)]_{0\leq i,j<n},
ℋ⁡(n,t)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}(n,t) :=detH⁡(n,t).\displaystyle:=\det H(n,t).

As a consequence of our main theorem, in Theorem 4.4 we obtain an explicit polynomial formula

(2) ℋ⁡(nk,t)=(−1)(k+1)​(k+2)2​tαk​(t−2)nk−2​(1+t+⋯+tk),\mathcal{H}(n_{k},t)=(-1)^{\frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}}t^{\alpha_{k}}(t-2)^{n_{k}-2}(1+t+\cdots+t^{k}),

for certain αk∈ℕ\alpha_{k}\in\mathbb{N}, which directly implies (1). Other applications of Theorem 4.2 include the determination of signs of detH⁡(n)\det H(n) and the degrees degt⁡ℋ⁡(n,t)\deg_{t}\mathcal{H}(n,t).

A significant part of the paper is devoted to the investigation of zero sets of ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t), which is a natural problem in view of the earlier discussion. One of the main results is Theorem 5.4, which shows that for every root of unity ζ\zeta of order d≥2d\geq 2, the determinants ℋ⁡(n,2​ζ)\mathcal{H}(n,2\zeta) vanish on long intervals centered at multiples of large powers of 22. This is complemented by Theorem 5.5, which gives quantitative bounds for the number of exceptional indices nn for which the corresponding determinant does not vanish, in particular implying the sparsity of these sets. On the other hand, we exhibit an infinite set of indices, different from nkn_{k}, such that ℋ⁡(n,2​ζ)≠0\mathcal{H}(n,2\zeta)\neq 0 (Theorem 5.10).

Recursive formulas for H𝐰​(n)H_{\mathbf{w}}(n) involve another sequence of determinants, closely related to Hankel determinants 𝒢𝐰​(n)\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) for the first-order difference

d𝐰​(n):=s𝐰​(n+1)−s𝐰​(n)d_{\mathbf{w}}(n):=s_{\mathbf{w}}(n+1)-s_{\mathbf{w}}(n)

Despite playing an auxiliary role, these determinants turn out to be quite interesting in their own right. In Theorem 3.4 we derive a closed product form for 𝒢𝐰​(n)\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n), which is controlled by the run lengths in the binary expansion of nn. As a special case, by choosing weights to be Jacobsthal numbers, we recover the result by Fokkink, Kraaikamp and Shallit [5, Theorem 2] concerning Hankel determinants for the period-doubling sequence and its bit-wise negation. We note that there appears to be a sign error in its original statement — a correct version is given in Proposition 3.9. For the polynomial specialization wj=tjw_{j}=t^{j}, in Corollary 3.10 we obtain an elegant formula for 𝒢𝐰​(n)\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n), giving a full description of the roots and their multiplicities.

The structure of the paper is as follows. Section 2 introduces the notation and conventions commonly used throughout the paper. In Section 3 we focus on the determinants 𝒢𝐰​(n)\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) associated with the first-order difference d𝐰d_{\mathbf{w}}. We provide the general product formula and the applications to special cases, including the period-doubling sequence and polynomial weights wj=tjw_{j}=t^{j}. In Section 4 we turn to the determinants ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n), associated with the weighted binary sum-of-digits function. The main result is the recursive relation for ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n), while the remainder of the section is devoted to its various implications. Section 5 is focused on vanishing and non-vanishing phenomena for the polynomials ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t). Finally, in Section 6 we collect several questions and problems suggested by the results obtained in the paper.

2. Notation and conventions

As we have already mentioned, we use the convention ℕ={0,1,2,…}\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,...\}. Moreover, we let ℕ+={1,2,…}\mathbb{N}_{+}=\{1,2,\ldots\} and, more generally, ℕ≥k={k,k+1,k+2,⋯}\mathbb{N}_{\geq k}=\{k,k+1,k+2,\cdots\} for k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. For n∈ℕ+n\in\mathbb{N}_{+} we will use the following notation for vectors and matrices that appear often throughout the paper:

  • •

    𝟎n\mathbf{0}_{n} — length nn column vector with all entries 00;

  • •

    𝟏n\mathbf{1}_{n} — length nn column vector with all entries 11;

  • •

    𝟎\mathbf{0} — matrix with all entries 00 of any size (implied by the context);

  • •

    JnJ_{n} — n×nn\times n matrix with all entries 11,

  • •

    KnK_{n} — n×nn\times n square matrix with 11s below the antidiagonal and 00s elsewhere;

  • •

    LnL_{n} — n×nn\times n square matrix with 11s on the antidiagonal and 00s elsewhere;

  • •

    MnM_{n} — n×nn\times n square matrix with 11s on and below the antidiagonal and 00s elsewhere.

More explicitly, the last three matrices are

Kn=[00⋯00⋰1⋰⋰01⋯1],Ln=[0⋯01⋰00⋰10⋯0],Mn=[00⋯10⋰1⋰⋰11⋯1].K_{n}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&\cdots&0\\ 0&&\iddots&1\\ \vdots&\iddots&\iddots&\vdots\\ 0&1&\cdots&1\end{bmatrix},\quad L_{n}=\begin{bmatrix}0&\cdots&0&1\\ \vdots&&\iddots&0\\ 0&\iddots&&\vdots\\ 1&0&\cdots&0\end{bmatrix},\quad M_{n}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&\cdots&1\\ 0&&\iddots&1\\ \vdots&\iddots&\iddots&\vdots\\ 1&1&\cdots&1\end{bmatrix}.

It is useful to note that

detLn=detMn=(−1)n⁡(n−1)2={1if ​n≡0,1(mod4),−1if ​n≡2,3(mod4).\det L_{n}=\det M_{n}=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }n\equiv 0,1\pmod{4},\\ -1&\text{if }n\equiv 2,3\pmod{4}.\end{cases}

We also use the standard notation ⊗\otimes for the Kronecker product of matrices (see for example [12, Chapter 20]). The property we are going to use the most is

(A⊗B)​(C⊗D)=(A​B)⊗(C​D)(A\otimes B)(C\otimes D)=(AB)\otimes(CD)

for matrices A,B,C,DA,B,C,D of appropriate size.

Below we list several further conventions:

  • •

    the rows and columns of matrices are indexed from 00;

  • •

    in a block matrix, non-bold 00 or 11 means a single entry;

  • •

    when writing block matrices, whose block sizes are symmetric along the diagonal, we sometimes suppress the indices of the matrices and write the heights of the blocks to the right of the matrix, for example:

    ††nicematrix-placeholder: bNiceArray (nicematrix)=††nicematrix-placeholder: NiceArray (nicematrix);\begin{bNiceArray}=\begin{NiceArray};
  • •

    when considering H𝐰​(n),G𝐰​(n)H_{\mathbf{w}}(n),G_{\mathbf{w}}(n) for 2k<n≤2k+12^{k}<n\leq 2^{k+1}, we sometimes specify 𝐰\mathbf{w} as the finite sequence of weights that actually appear in the matrices, that is, 𝐰=(w0,w1,…,wk+1)\mathbf{w}=(w_{0},w_{1},\ldots,w_{k+1}).

3. Formulas for the determinants 𝒢𝐰​(n)\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)

In this section, we consider Hankel matrices and determinants associated with the first-difference sequence (d𝐰​(n))n≥0(d_{\mathbf{w}}(n))_{n\geq 0}, that is,

G𝐰​(n)\displaystyle G_{\mathbf{w}}(n) :=[d𝐰​(i+j)]0≤i,j<n,\displaystyle:=[d_{\mathbf{w}}(i+j)]_{0\leq i,j<n},
𝒢𝐰​(n)\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) :=detG𝐰​(n).\displaystyle:=\det G_{\mathbf{w}}(n).

We derive general formulas for 𝒢𝐰​(n)\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) and later apply them to special weights 𝐰\mathbf{w}. In particular, we obtain as a corollary the aforementioned result from [5] on Hankel determinants of the period-doubling sequence.

We also consider related n×nn\times n matrices G~𝐰​(n)\widetilde{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) and their determinants:

G~𝐰​(n)\displaystyle\widetilde{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) :=[d𝐰​(0)⋯d𝐰​(n−2)1d𝐰​(n−1)⋯d𝐰​(2​n−3)1],\displaystyle:=\begin{bmatrix}d_{\mathbf{w}}(0)&\cdots&d_{\mathbf{w}}(n-2)&1\\ \vdots&&\vdots&\vdots\\ d_{\mathbf{w}}(n-1)&\cdots&d_{\mathbf{w}}(2n-3)&1\\ \end{bmatrix},
𝒢~𝐰​(n)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) :=detG~𝐰​(n).\displaystyle:=\det\widetilde{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n).

In other words, G~𝐰​(n)\widetilde{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) is obtained from G𝐰​(n)G_{\mathbf{w}}(n) by replacing all entries in the rightmost column with 11s. Their determinants will appear in Section 4 in the recursion for ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n).

3.1. Recurrence relations

To begin, we express in a more explicit way the entries d𝐰​(m)d_{\mathbf{w}}(m). If we write m+1=2k+1​l+2km+1=2^{k+1}l+2^{k} for some k,l∈ℕk,l\in\mathbb{N}, then

d𝐰​(m)=s𝐰​(2k+1​l+2k)−s𝐰​(2k+1​l+∑j=0k−12j)=wk−∑j=0k−1wj.d_{\mathbf{w}}(m)=s_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k+1}l+2^{k})-s_{\mathbf{w}}\left(2^{k+1}l+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}2^{j}\right)=w_{k}-\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}w_{j}.

We can rewrite this equality in terms of the sequence 𝐮=(un)n≥0\mathbf{u}=(u_{n})_{n\geq 0}, defined by

u0\displaystyle u_{0} :=w0,\displaystyle:=w_{0},
un\displaystyle u_{n} :=wn−2​wn−1,n≥1.\displaystyle:=w_{n}-2w_{n-1},\quad n\geq 1.

Then we have the expression

(3) d𝐰​(m)=∑i=0ν2​(m+1)ui,d_{\mathbf{w}}(m)=\sum_{i=0}^{\nu_{2}(m+1)}u_{i},

where ν2\nu_{2} denotes the 22-adic valuation. For example, we have

G𝐰​(4)=[u0u0+u1u0u0+u1+u2u0+u1u0u0+u1+u2u0u0u0+u1+u2u0u0+u1u0+u1+u2u0u0+u1u0].G_{\mathbf{w}}(4)=\begin{bmatrix}u_{0}&u_{0}+u_{1}&u_{0}&u_{0}+u_{1}+u_{2}\\ u_{0}+u_{1}&u_{0}&u_{0}+u_{1}+u_{2}&u_{0}\\ u_{0}&u_{0}+u_{1}+u_{2}&u_{0}&u_{0}+u_{1}\\ u_{0}+u_{1}+u_{2}&u_{0}&u_{0}+u_{1}&u_{0}\\ \end{bmatrix}.

Conversely, if we start with 𝐮\mathbf{u} and define d𝐰​(m)d_{\mathbf{w}}(m) by (3), then the sequence of weights 𝐰\mathbf{w} can be recovered using the relations

w0\displaystyle w_{0} =u0,\displaystyle=u_{0},
wn\displaystyle w_{n} =∑j=0n2n−j​uj,n≥1.\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{n}2^{n-j}u_{j},\quad n\geq 1.

As a first auxiliary result, we obtain a recurrence relation for the matrices G𝐰​(n)G_{\mathbf{w}}(n).

Proposition 3.1.

For all k∈ℕ,n∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N},n\in\mathbb{N}_{+} we have

G𝐰​(2k​n)=Jn⊗G𝐰​(2k)+G𝐰′​(n)⊗L2k,\displaystyle G_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k}n)=J_{n}\otimes G_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k})+G_{\mathbf{w}^{\prime}}(n)\otimes L_{2^{k}},

where 𝐰′=(wj′)j≥0\mathbf{w}^{\prime}=(w_{j}^{\prime})_{j\geq 0} depends only on kk and is defined by

wj′=wj+k−2j​wk.w^{\prime}_{j}=w_{j+k}-2^{j}w_{k}.
Proof.

Write G𝐰​(2k​n)G_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k}n) as an n×nn\times n block matrix:

G𝐰​(2k​n)=[G0G1⋯Gn−1G1G2⋯GnGn−1Gn⋯G2​n−2],G_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k}n)=\begin{bmatrix}G_{0}&G_{1}&\cdots&G_{n-1}\\ G_{1}&G_{2}&\cdots&G_{n}\\ \vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\ G_{n-1}&G_{n}&\cdots&G_{2n-2}\end{bmatrix},

where the blocks GlG_{l} have size 2k×2k2^{k}\times 2^{k}. Consider the entry at position (i,j)(i,j) in GlG_{l}, that is, d𝐰​(2k​l+i+j)d_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k}l+i+j). If i+j≠2k−1i+j\neq 2^{k}-1, then ν2​(2k​l+i+j+1)=ν2​(i+j+1)\nu_{2}(2^{k}l+i+j+1)=\nu_{2}(i+j+1), so by (3) we get d𝐰​(2k​l+i+j)=d𝐰​(i+j)d_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k}l+i+j)=d_{\mathbf{w}}(i+j). Otherwise, if i+j=2k−1i+j=2^{k}-1, then

d𝐰​(2k​l+i+j)=∑m=0k+ν2​(l+1)um=d𝐰​(2k−1)+∑m=1ν2​(l+1)uk+m=d𝐰​(i+j)+d𝐰′​(l),d_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k}l+i+j)=\sum_{m=0}^{k+\nu_{2}(l+1)}u_{m}=d_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k}-1)+\sum_{m=1}^{\nu_{2}(l+1)}u_{k+m}=d_{\mathbf{w}}(i+j)+d_{\mathbf{w}^{\prime}}(l),

This means that

Gl=G𝐰​(2k)+d𝐰′​(l)​L2k,G_{l}=G_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k})+d_{\mathbf{w}^{\prime}}(l)L_{2^{k}},

and the result follows. ∎

We now apply this identity to obtain a recursion for 𝒢𝐰​(n)\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) and 𝒢~𝐰​(n)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(n). This is a generalization of [5, Lemmas 8, 9].

Proposition 3.2.

Let n∈ℕ≥2n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} be such that 2k<n≤2k+12^{k}<n\leq 2^{k+1}. The following recursive formulas hold.

  1. (a)

    If 2k<n≤3⋅2k−12^{k}<n\leq 3\cdot 2^{k-1}, then

    𝒢𝐰​(n)\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) =(−1)n​(wk+1−2​wk)2​n−2k+1​𝒢𝐰​(2k+1−n),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n}(w_{k+1}-2w_{k})^{2n-2^{k+1}}\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k+1}-n),
    𝒢~𝐰​(n)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) =(−1)n​(wk+1−2​wk)2​n−2k+1−1​𝒢~𝐰​(2k+1−n+1).\displaystyle=(-1)^{n}(w_{k+1}-2w_{k})^{2n-2^{k+1}-1}\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k+1}-n+1).

Remark 3.6.

Theorem 3.4 shows that the structure of 𝒢𝐰​(n)\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) can be seen from the pattern of consecutive blocks in the binary expansion of nn. More precisely, the relevant indices kik_{i} and exponents αi,j\alpha_{i,j} are determined by the lengths of these blocks, so the factorization reflects the 2-adic structure of nn rather than its size alone.

It should be possible to obtain a similar prodduct formula for the determinants 𝒢~𝐰​(n)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(n). However, this seems more tricky, due to the additional “+1+1” in the index in Proposition 3.2(a), which makes the indices harder to control when applying the proposition repeatedly. Instead, we settle for the following qualitative description, which will be sufficient for our purposes.

Proposition 3.7.

Let n∈ℕ≥2n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} and let k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} be such that 2k<n≤2k+12^{k}<n\leq 2^{k+1}. Then we have the following:

  1. (a)

    𝒢~𝐰​(n)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) is, up to sign, a product of n−1n-1 factors of the form (wl−2l−j​wj)(w_{l}-2^{l-j}w_{j}), where 0≤j<l≤k+10\leq j<l\leq k+1;

  2. (b)

    the total multiplicity of factors with l=k+1l=k+1 is equal to 2​n−2k+1−12n-2^{k+1}-1.

Proof.

We prove (a) and (b) simultaneously by induction on nn. We have 𝒢~𝐰​(1)=1\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(1)=1 so both statements hold for n=1n=1. Now, let n≥2n\geq 2 and consider two cases. If 2k<n≤3⋅2k−12^{k}<n\leq 3\cdot 2^{k-1}, then our claim follows directly from Proposition 3.2(a). If 3⋅2k−1<n≤2k+13\cdot 2^{k-1}<n\leq 2^{k+1}, then by Proposition 3.2(b) we have

𝒢~𝐰​(n)=22​n−3⋅2k−1​(wk+1−2​wk)2k​𝒢~𝐰′​(n−2k),\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)=2^{2n-3\cdot 2^{k}-1}(w_{k+1}-2w_{k})^{2^{k}}\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w^{\prime}}}(n-2^{k}),

where 𝐰′=(w0,w1,…,wk−1,12​wk+1)\mathbf{w}^{\prime}=(w_{0},w_{1},\ldots,w_{k-1},\frac{1}{2}w_{k+1}). The inductive assumption says that the total multiplicity of factors of the form (12​wk+1−2k−j​wj)(\frac{1}{2}w_{k+1}-2^{k-j}w_{j}) in 𝒢~𝐰′​(n−2k)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w^{\prime}}}(n-2^{k}) is

2​(n−2k)−2k−1=2​n−3⋅2k−1.2(n-2^{k})-2^{k}-1=2n-3\cdot 2^{k}-1.

Distributing the power 22​n−3⋅2k−12^{2n-3\cdot 2^{k}-1} over these factors and taking (wk+1−2​wk)2k(w_{k+1}-2w_{k})^{2^{k}} into account, we again obtain our claim. ∎

3.3. Special cases

We now give some applications of Theorem 3.4. The first one relies on a simple but somewhat unexpected connection, which we state as a proposition. More precisely, the period-doubling sequence 𝐝=(dn)n≥0\mathbf{d}=(d_{n})_{n\geq 0} and its bit-wise negation 𝐝¯=(d¯n)n≥0\bar{\mathbf{d}}=(\bar{d}_{n})_{n\geq 0} turn out to be instances of 𝐝𝐰\mathbf{d}_{\mathbf{w}} where the weights are (shifted) Jacobsthal numbers. We follow the definition from [5], where

dn:=(ν2​(n+1)+1)mod2.d_{n}:=(\nu_{2}(n+1)+1)\bmod{2}.

We note that the variant with 00s and 11s swapped (𝐝\mathbf{d} becomes 𝐝¯\bar{\mathbf{d}} and vice versa) seems to be more common. Also, recall that Jacobsthal numbers are defined by J⁡(0)=0,J⁡(1)=1J(0)=0,J(1)=1 and J⁡(n+2)=J⁡(n+1)+2​J​(n)J(n+2)=J(n+1)+2J(n) for n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}.

Proposition 3.8.

We have the following:

  1. (a)

    If 𝐰=(J⁡(j+1))j≥0\mathbf{w}=(J(j+1))_{j\geq 0}, then 𝐝𝐰\mathbf{d}_{\mathbf{w}} is the period-doubling sequence 𝐝\mathbf{d};

  2. (b)

    If 𝐰=(J⁡(j))j≥0\mathbf{w}=(J(j))_{j\geq 0}, then 𝐝𝐰\mathbf{d}_{\mathbf{w}} is the bit-wise negation 𝐝¯\bar{\mathbf{d}} of the period-doubling sequence.

Proof.

In the case (a) we have u0=J1=1u_{0}=J_{1}=1 and uj=J⁡(j+1)−2​J​(j)=(−1)ju_{j}=J(j+1)-2J(j)=(-1)^{j} for j≥1j\geq 1, which is a well-known identity. It follows that

d𝐰​(n)=∑j=0ν2​(n+1)(−1)j=(ν2​(n+1)+1)mod2=dn.d_{\mathbf{w}}(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{\nu_{2}(n+1)}(-1)^{j}=(\nu_{2}(n+1)+1)\bmod{2}=d_{n}.

In the case (b), we have u0=J0=0u_{0}=J_{0}=0 and uj=J⁡(j)−2​J​(j−1)=(−1)j−1u_{j}=J(j)-2J(j-1)=(-1)^{j-1} for j≥1j\geq 1. A similar computation leads to d𝐰​(n)=d¯nd_{\mathbf{w}}(n)=\bar{d}_{n}. ∎

As a corollary, we obtain a slight generalization of the result by Fokkink, Kraaikamp and Shallit [5, Theorem 2] (and more general Theorem 10 from the same paper) concerning Hankel determinants for the period-doubling sequence. There appears to be a small mistake in the original statement of the latter theorem, namely the conditions modulo 44 governing the sign of the determinant are shifted by 11.

Proposition 3.9.

Let n∈ℕ+n\in\mathbb{N}_{+} and, with the notation of Theorem 3.4, put

l=max1≤i≤sli,Aj=∑i:li≥jsαi,j.l=\max_{1\leq i\leq s}l_{i},\qquad A_{j}=\sum_{i:\,l_{i}\geq j}^{s}\alpha_{i,j}.

Then we have the following:

  1. (a)

    The nnth Hankel determinant for the period-doubling sequence 𝐝\mathbf{d} is

    (−1)(n−1)​(n−2)2​J​(l1+1)​∏j=1lJ​(j)Aj.(-1)^{\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2}}J(l_{1}+1)\prod_{j=1}^{l}J(j)^{A_{j}}.
  2. (b)

    The nnth Hankel determinant for the bit-wise negation 𝐝¯\bar{\mathbf{d}} of the period-doubling sequence is

    (−1)n⁡(n−1)2​J​(l1)​∏j=1lJ​(j)Aj.(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}J(l_{1})\prod_{j=1}^{l}J(j)^{A_{j}}.

    In particular, the determinant is nonzero if and only if nn is even.

Proof.

In case (a), put 𝐰=(J⁡(j+1))j≥0\mathbf{w}=(J(j+1))_{j\geq 0}. The product over i,ji,j in Theorem 3.4 consists of factors of the form

wki−2j​wki−j=J⁡(ki+1)−2j​J​(ki+1−j)=(−1)ki+1−j​J​(j).w_{k_{i}}-2^{j}w_{k_{i}-j}=J(k_{i}+1)-2^{j}J(k_{i}+1-j)=(-1)^{k_{i}+1-j}J(j).

After rearranging, we get the product as in the statement (up to sign). The sign equals −1-1 raised to the power

n⁡(n−1)2+∑i=1s∑j=1li(ki+1−j)​αi,j.\frac{n(n-1)}{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\sum_{j=1}^{l_{i}}(k_{i}+1-j)\alpha_{i,j}.

The only odd αi,j\alpha_{i,j} is α1,l1=1\alpha_{1,l_{1}}=1, which only occurs when l1≥2l_{1}\geq 2, i.e., nn is even. The corresponding summand equals 11, and we obtain the sign as in the statement.

The proof of (b) is similar. This time, the factors are

wki−2j​wki−j=J⁡(ki)−2j​J​(ki−j)=(−1)ki−j​J​(j),w_{k_{i}}-2^{j}w_{k_{i}-j}=J(k_{i})-2^{j}J(k_{i}-j)=(-1)^{k_{i}-j}J(j),

and the sign equals −1-1 raised to the power

All summands are even, and we again obtain the desired formula. ∎

We now apply Theorem 3.4 to the weights wj=tjw_{j}=t^{j}, where we adopt the notation

𝒢⁡(n,t):=𝒢𝐰​(n)for ​𝐰=(tj)j≥0.\mathcal{G}(n,t):=\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\qquad\text{for }\mathbf{w}=(t^{j})_{j\geq 0}.

The resulting characterization of the roots 𝒢⁡(n,t)\mathcal{G}(n,t) will play a role in Section 5.

Corollary 3.10.

Let n∈ℕ+n\in\mathbb{N}_{+} and, with the notation of Theorem 3.4, put

A=l1+∑i=1s∑j=1l1(ki−j)αi,j,l=max1≤i≤sli,Aj=∑i:li≥jsαi,j.A=l_{1}+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\sum_{j=1}^{l_{1}}(k_{i}-j)\alpha_{i,j},\qquad l=\max_{1\leq i\leq s}l_{i},\qquad A_{j}=\sum_{i:\,l_{i}\geq j}^{s}\alpha_{i,j}.

4. Formulas for the determinants ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)

The main goal of this section is to derive formulas for the determinants ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n). In the general case we give a set of recursive formulas, involving a sequence of determinants of certain auxiliary matrices. For special choices of weights 𝐰\mathbf{w} and indices nn we provide explicit expressions, including (1) and (2). The overall approach is similar as in the previous section, although some additional complications arise.

4.1. Recurrence relations

We first give a recurrence relation satisfied by the matrices H𝐰​(n)H_{\mathbf{w}}(n). In its formulation, we use the notation

F𝐰​(n):=G𝐰​(n)−w0​Jn=[d𝐰​(i+j)−w0]0≤i,j<n.F_{\mathbf{w}}(n):=G_{\mathbf{w}}(n)-w_{0}J_{n}=[d_{\mathbf{w}}(i+j)-w_{0}]_{0\leq i,j<n}.
Proposition 4.1.

where 𝐰(k)=(wk,wk+1,…)\mathbf{w}^{(k)}=(w_{k},w_{k+1},\ldots) denotes the kk-fold shift of 𝐰\mathbf{w}.

where the blocks HlH_{l} have size 2k×2k2^{k}\times 2^{k}. The entry at position (i,j)(i,j) in HlH_{l} is

s𝐰​(2k​l+i+j)={s𝐰(k)​(l)+s𝐰​(i+j)if ​i+j<2m,s𝐰(k)​(l+1)+s𝐰​(i+j)−wkif ​i+j≥2m.s_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k}l+i+j)=\begin{cases}s_{\mathbf{w}^{(k)}}(l)+s_{\mathbf{w}}(i+j)&\text{if }i+j<2^{m},\\ s_{\mathbf{w}^{(k)}}(l+1)+s_{\mathbf{w}}(i+j)-w_{k}&\text{if }i+j\geq 2^{m}.\end{cases}

This means that

and the result follows. ∎

4.2. Special cases

We start with the aforementioned polynomial generalization of (1). As before, we consider the sequence of indices nk=⌈2k+2/3⌉n_{k}=\lceil 2^{k+2}/3\rceil, which can be equivalently defined by n0=2n_{0}=2 and

(9) nk=2k+1−nk−1+1,k≥1,n_{k}=2^{k+1}-n_{k-1}+1,\quad k\geq 1,

or nk=2​nk−1−(kmod2)n_{k}=2n_{k-1}-(k\bmod{2}).

Theorem 4.4.

For all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} we have

ℋ⁡(nk,t)=(−1)(k+1)​(k+2)2​tαk​(t−2)nk−2​(1+t+⋯+tk),\mathcal{H}(n_{k},t)=(-1)^{\frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}}t^{\alpha_{k}}(t-2)^{n_{k}-2}(1+t+\cdots+t^{k}),

where

αk=(k−1)​nk+2−⌊k+12⌋.\alpha_{k}=(k-1)n_{k}+2-\left\lfloor\frac{k+1}{2}\right\rfloor.

In particular, Hankel determinants for the usual binary sum of digits satisfy

ℋ⁡(nk,1)=(−1)(k+2)​(k+3)2​(k+1).\mathcal{H}(n_{k},1)=(-1)^{\frac{(k+2)(k+3)}{2}}(k+1).
Proof.

We use induction on kk to simultaneously prove the expression for ℋ⁡(nk,t)\mathcal{H}(n_{k},t) and

𝒢~​(nk,t)=(−1)(k+2)​(k+3)2​tαk​(t−2)nk−1.\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}(n_{k},t)=(-1)^{\frac{(k+2)(k+3)}{2}}\>t^{\alpha_{k}}(t-2)^{n_{k}-1}.

Our claim holds for k=0,1k=0,1 by direct computation.

Now, let k≥2k\geq 2 and assume that both formulas are true for k−1k-1. Since 2k<nk≤3⋅2k−12^{k}<n_{k}\leq 3\cdot 2^{k-1}, by Theorem 4.2(a) we get

[ℋ⁡(nk,t)𝒢~​(nk,t)]=(−1)nk​(tk​(t−2))nk−nk−1​[−1(−1)nk​tkt−201]​[ℋ⁡(nk−1,t)𝒢~​(nk−1,t)].\begin{bmatrix}\mathcal{H}(n_{k},t)\\ \widetilde{\mathcal{G}}(n_{k},t)\end{bmatrix}=(-1)^{n_{k}}\left(t^{k}(t-2)\right)^{n_{k}-n_{k-1}}\begin{bmatrix}-1&(-1)^{n_{k}}\frac{t^{k}}{t-2}\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathcal{H}(n_{k-1},t)\\ \widetilde{\mathcal{G}}(n_{k-1},t)\end{bmatrix}.

Using the inductive assumption together with nk≡k(mod2)n_{k}\equiv k\pmod{2} and αk=αk−1+k⁡(nk−nk−1)\alpha_{k}=\alpha_{k-1}+k(n_{k}-n_{k-1}), we get the formulas for kk. ∎

The main reason behind the existence of such a nice formula seems to be the fact that at each step of the induction, we used part (a) of Theorem 4.2 so the weights wj=tjw_{j}=t^{j} did not change at any point.

In the next result, we give more complicated, although still compact formulas for ℋ⁡(2m+ε,1)\mathcal{H}(2^{m}+\varepsilon,1) for ε∈{−1,0,1}\varepsilon\in\{-1,0,1\}.

Proposition 4.5.

For any m∈ℕ≥2m\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} we have

ℋ⁡(2m,1)=∑j=1m2j−12j−1​∏j=1m(2j−1)2m−j,\mathcal{H}(2^{m},1)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{2^{j-1}}{2^{j}-1}\prod_{j=1}^{m}(2^{j}-1)^{2^{m-j}},
ℋ(2m+1,1)=−(1+∑j=1m2j−12j−1)∏j=1m(2j−1)2m−j,\mathcal{H}(2^{m}+1,1)=-\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{2^{j-1}}{2^{j}-1}\right)\prod_{j=1}^{m}(2^{j}-1)^{2^{m-j}},

and

ℋ⁡(2m−1,1)=(2m−1−1)​(1+∑j=1m−12j−12j−1)​∏j=1m−2(2j−1)2m−j.\mathcal{H}(2^{m}-1,1)=(2^{m-1}-1)\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac{2^{j-1}}{2^{j}-1}\right)\prod_{j=1}^{m-2}(2^{j}-1)^{2^{m-j}}.

All three formulas are valid for m=2m=2, so assume m≥3m\geq 3. By repeated application of Proposition (b), for k≥2k\geq 2 and l≥1l\geq 1 we get

(10) [h⁡(2k+l,1,x)g~​(2k+l,1,x)]=12l​∏j=1l(22−j​x−4)2k+l−j​[1∑j=0l−11x/2j−201]​[h⁡(2k,1,x2l)g~​(2k,1,x2l)].\begin{bmatrix}h(2^{k+l},1,x)\\ \widetilde{g}(2^{k+l},1,x)\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2^{l}}\prod_{j=1}^{l}(2^{2-j}x-4)^{2^{k+l-j}}\begin{bmatrix}1&\sum\limits_{j=0}^{l-1}\frac{1}{x/2^{j}-2}\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}h(2^{k},1,\frac{x}{2^{l}})\\ \widetilde{g}(2^{k},1,\frac{x}{2^{l}})\end{bmatrix}.

h⁡(2m,1,1)=\displaystyle h(2^{m},1,1)= 12m−2​∏j=1m−2(22−j−4)2m−j\displaystyle\frac{1}{2^{m-2}}\prod_{j=1}^{m-2}(2^{2-j}-4)^{2^{m-j}}
[h⁡(4,1,12m−2)+g~​(4,1,12m−2)​∑j=0m−32j−12j−1].\displaystyle\left[h\left(4,1,\frac{1}{2^{m-2}}\right)+\widetilde{g}\left(4,1,\frac{1}{2^{m-2}}\right)\sum\limits_{j=0}^{m-3}\frac{2^{j-1}}{2^{j}-1}\right].

Taking into account that h⁡(4,1,y)=(y−2)​(3​y−8)h(4,1,y)=(y-2)(3y-8) and g~​(4,1,y)=(y−2)2​(y−4),\widetilde{g}(4,1,y)=(y-2)^{2}(y-4), after some algebraic manipulation we get the desired formula

(11) ℋ⁡(2m,1)=h⁡(2m,1,1)=∑j=1m2j−12j−1​∏j=1m(2j−1)2m−j.\mathcal{H}(2^{m},1)=h(2^{m},1,1)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{2^{j-1}}{2^{j}-1}\prod_{j=1}^{m}(2^{j}-1)^{2^{m-j}}.

To obtain the formula for ℋ⁡(2m+1,1)\mathcal{H}(2^{m}+1,1), we apply Proposition (a) to k=m,n=2m+1k=m,n=2^{m}+1, and t=x=1t=x=1, obtaining

(12) h⁡(2m+1,1,1)=−h⁡(2m,1,1)+g⁡(2m,1,1).h(2^{m}+1,1,1)=-h(2^{m},1,1)+g(2^{m},1,1).

From (10) we get

g(2m,1,1)=12m−2∏j=1m−2(22−j−4)2m−jg(4,1,12m−2)=−∏j=1m(2j−1)2m−j.g(2^{m},1,1)=\frac{1}{2^{m-2}}\prod_{j=1}^{m-2}(2^{2-j}-4)^{2^{m-j}}\,g\!\left(4,1,\frac{1}{2^{m-2}}\right)=-\prod_{j=1}^{m}(2^{j}-1)^{2^{m-j}}.

Substituting this and (11) into (12), we get

h(2m+1,1,1)=−(1+∑j=1m2j−12j−1)∏j=1m(2j−1)2m−j.h(2^{m}+1,1,1)=-\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{2^{j-1}}{2^{j}-1}\right)\prod_{j=1}^{m}(2^{j}-1)^{2^{m-j}}.

The proof of the last identity relies on the formula

[h⁡(2k+l−1,1,x)g~​(2k+l−1,1,x)]=12l​∏j=1l(22−j​x−4)2k+l−j​[1∑j=0l−11x/2j−201]​[h⁡(2k−1,1,x2l)g~​(2k−1,1,x2l)],\begin{bmatrix}h(2^{k+l}-1,1,x)\\ \widetilde{g}(2^{k+l}-1,1,x)\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2^{l}}\prod_{j=1}^{l}(2^{2-j}x-4)^{2^{k+l-j}}\begin{bmatrix}1&\sum\limits_{j=0}^{l-1}\frac{1}{x/2^{j}-2}\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}h(2^{k}-1,1,\frac{x}{2^{l}})\\ \widetilde{g}(2^{k}-1,1,\frac{x}{2^{l}})\end{bmatrix},

which again follows from Proposition (b). The details are left for the reader to verify. ∎

Based on the form of the values of ℋ⁡(2m+k,1)\mathcal{H}(2^{m}+k,1) for k=−1,0,1k=-1,0,1 given in Proposition 4.5, we formulate the following conjecture.

Conjecture 4.6.

For every fixed integer k≥0k\geq 0 there exist integers m0=m0​(k)≥0m_{0}=m_{0}(k)\geq 0 and r=r⁡(k)≥0r=r(k)\geq 0, a sign εk∈{±1}\varepsilon_{k}\in\{\pm 1\}, a polynomial Pk​(X)∈ℚ​[X]P_{k}(X)\in\mathbb{Q}[X], and a constant ck∈ℚc_{k}\in\mathbb{Q} such that for all m≥m0​(k)m\geq m_{0}(k) we have

ℋ⁡(2m+k,1)=εk​Pk​(2m)​(ck+∑j=1m−r2j−12j−1)​∏j=1m−r(2j−1)2m−r−j.\mathcal{H}(2^{m}+k,1)=\varepsilon_{k}\,P_{k}(2^{m})\left(c_{k}+\sum_{j=1}^{m-r}\frac{2^{j-1}}{2^{j}-1}\right)\prod_{j=1}^{m-r}(2^{j}-1)^{2^{m-r-j}}.

Moreover, the polynomial Pk​(2m)P_{k}(2^{m}) and the shift r⁡(k)r(k) are determined by the binary expansion of kk and the sequence of “branches” encountered when repeatedly applying Theorem 4.2.

Another interesting feature of the sequence (ℋ⁡(n,1))n≥1(\mathcal{H}(n,1))_{n\geq 1}, suggested by experimental computations, is that the sequence of absolute values (|ℋ⁡(n,1)|)n≥2(|\mathcal{H}(n,1)|)_{n\geq 2} contains long monotone increasing and decreasing subsequences. Moreover, local maxima and minima seem to occur at the indices 2k+12^{k}+1 and nkn_{k} (defined by (9)), respectively. Motivated by this observation, we formulate the following conjecture.

Conjecture 4.7.

The sequence of absolute values (|ℋ⁡(n,1)|)n≥2(|\mathcal{H}(n,1)|)_{n\geq 2} is:

  1. (1)

    strictly increasing in each interval [nk,2k+1+1][n_{k},2^{k+1}+1];

  2. (2)

    strictly decreasing in each interval [2k+1+1,nk+1][2^{k+1}+1,n_{k+1}].

In particular, for each k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} we have

|ℋ⁡(2k+1,1)|=maxn≤2k+1⁡|ℋ⁡(n,1)|.|\mathcal{H}(2^{k}+1,1)|=\max_{n\leq 2^{k}+1}|\mathcal{H}(n,1)|.

4.3. Degree and leading coefficient

We now study the polynomials ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) in terms of their degree and leading coefficient. In fact, we give a more general result concerning the weighted degree of ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n).

Let PP be a polynomial in variables w0,w1,…,wlw_{0},w_{1},\ldots,w_{l}:

P(w0,w1,…,wl)=∑a=(a0,a1,…,al)∈𝒜caw0a0w1a1⋯wlal,P(w_{0},w_{1},\ldots,w_{l})=\sum_{a=(a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{l})\in\mathcal{A}}c_{a}w_{0}^{a_{0}}w_{1}^{a_{1}}\cdots w_{l}^{a_{l}},

where 𝒜⊂ℕl+1\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{N}^{l+1} is finite and ca∈ℂ∖{0}c_{a}\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}. Its weighted degree D⁡(P)D(P), where wjw_{j} is assigned weight jj, is defined by

D⁡(P):=max⁡{∑j=0lj​aj:a∈𝒜}.D(P):=\max\left\{\sum_{j=0}^{l}ja_{j}:\>a\in\mathcal{A}\right\}.

If there is precisely one monomial satisfying D(caw0a0w1a1⋯wlal)=D(P)D(c_{a}w_{0}^{a_{0}}w_{1}^{a_{1}}\cdots w_{l}^{a_{l}})=D(P) we will say that it is the leading monomial of PP (this is not standard terminology).

Now, define

Dn:=D⁡(ℋ𝐰​(n)).D_{n}:=D(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)).

The weights are chosen in such a way that degt⁡ℋ⁡(n,t)\deg_{t}\mathcal{H}(n,t) is expected to be equal to DnD_{n}. The equality is not obvious due to potential cancellation in ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t), however, the following proposition shows that it indeed holds.

Proposition 4.8.

For n∈ℕ≥2n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} we have the following:

  1. (a)

    for k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that 2k<n≤2k+12^{k}<n\leq 2^{k+1} we have

    Dn={D2k+1−n+1+(2​n−2k+1−1)​(k+1)+1if ​n≤3⋅2k−1,Dn−2k+2​n+2k​(k−2)if ​n>3⋅2k−1;D_{n}=\begin{cases}D_{2^{k+1}-n+1}+(2n-2^{k+1}-1)(k+1)+1&\text{if }n\leq 3\cdot 2^{k-1},\\ D_{n-2^{k}}+2n+2^{k}(k-2)&\text{if }n>3\cdot 2^{k-1};\end{cases}
  2. (b)

    the leading coefficient of ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) belongs to {1,−1}\{1,-1\};

  3. (c)

    degt⁡ℋ⁡(n,t)=Dn\deg_{t}\mathcal{H}(n,t)=D_{n}.

Proof.

Let En:=D⁡(𝒢~𝐰​(n))E_{n}:=D(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)). Let n≥2n\geq 2 and kk be such that 2k<n≤2k+12^{k}<n\leq 2^{k+1}. We simultaneously prove the following statements by induction:

  1. (i)

    Dn=En+k−1D_{n}=E_{n}+k-1;

  2. (ii)

    ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) has a leading monomial and the coefficient of this monomial is ±1\pm 1.

Both statements hold for n<5n<5, and thus let n≥5n\geq 5. We will use the notation A𝐰​(n),B𝐰​(n),C𝐰​(n)A_{\mathbf{w}}(n),B_{\mathbf{w}}(n),C_{\mathbf{w}}(n) from Theorem 4.2. In particular, we have

D​(A𝐰​(n))\displaystyle D(A_{\mathbf{w}}(n)) =(2​n−2k+1−1)​(k+1)\displaystyle=(2n-2^{k+1}-1)(k+1)
D⁡(A𝐰​(n)​C𝐰​(n))\displaystyle D(A_{\mathbf{w}}(n)C_{\mathbf{w}}(n)) =(2​n−2k+1)​(k+1)−2,\displaystyle=(2n-2^{k+1})(k+1)-2,
D​(B𝐰​(n))\displaystyle D(B_{\mathbf{w}}(n)) =2k​(k+1),\displaystyle=2^{k}(k+1),
D⁡(B𝐰​(n)​C𝐰​(n))\displaystyle D(B_{\mathbf{w}}(n)C_{\mathbf{w}}(n)) =(2k+1)​(k+1)−2.\displaystyle=(2^{k}+1)(k+1)-2.

If 2k<n≤3⋅2k−12^{k}<n\leq 3\cdot 2^{k-1}, then 2k−1<2k+1−n+1≤2k2^{k-1}<2^{k+1}-n+1\leq 2^{k} and the inductive assumption implies

D⁡(A𝐰​(n)​ℋ𝐰​(2k+1−n+1))=D⁡(A𝐰​(n)​C𝐰​(n)​𝒢~𝐰​(2k+1−n+1))−1.D(A_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k+1}-n+1))=D(A_{\mathbf{w}}(n)C_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k+1}-n+1))-1.

Hence, by Theorem 4.2(a) we get

Dn=D⁡(A𝐰​(n)​C𝐰​(n)​𝒢~𝐰​(2k+1−n+1))=En+k−1.D_{n}=D(A_{\mathbf{w}}(n)C_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k+1}-n+1))=E_{n}+k-1.

Combining these two equalities, we also obtain the first case in (a).

To see that (ii) holds, note that by Proposition 3.7, the polynomial 𝒢~𝐰​(2k+1−n+1)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k+1}-n+1) has a leading monomial with coefficient ±1\pm 1. This remains true for the polynomial A𝐰​(n)​C𝐰​(n)​𝒢~𝐰​(2k+1−n+1)A_{\mathbf{w}}(n)C_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k+1}-n+1), and its leading monomial becomes the leading monomial in ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) (up to sign).

In the case 3⋅2k−1<n≤2k+13\cdot 2^{k-1}<n\leq 2^{k+1} we have 2k−1<n−2k≤2k2^{k-1}<n-2^{k}\leq 2^{k}. We need a bit more caution when comparing weighted degrees of the polynomials B𝐰​(n)​ℋ𝐰′​(n−2k)B_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w^{\prime}}}(n-2^{k}) and B𝐰​(n)​C𝐰​(n)​𝒢~𝐰′​(n−2k)B_{\mathbf{w}}(n)C_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w^{\prime}}}(n-2^{k}) appearing in Theorem 4.2(b). By Proposition 3.7, the leading monomial in 𝒢~𝐰​(n−2k)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(n-2^{k}) contains wkw_{k} with multiplicity 2​n−3⋅2k−12n-3\cdot 2^{k}-1. It follows that

D⁡(𝒢~𝐰′​(n−2k))=En−2k+2​n−3⋅2k−1.D(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w^{\prime}}}(n-2^{k}))=E_{n-2^{k}}+2n-3\cdot 2^{k}-1.

At the same time, wkw_{k} occurs in ℋ𝐰​(n−2k)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n-2^{k}) precisely at positions (i,j)(i,j) such that i+j≥2ki+j\geq 2^{k}, which are contained in a square submatrix of size 2​n−3⋅2k−12n-3\cdot 2^{k}-1. Hence, after the substitution wk↦12​wk+1w_{k}\mapsto\frac{1}{2}w_{k+1} we get

D⁡(ℋ𝐰′​(n−2k))≤Dn−2k+2​n−3⋅2k−1.D(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w^{\prime}}}(n-2^{k}))\leq D_{n-2^{k}}+2n-3\cdot 2^{k}-1.

Together with the inductive assumption, this leads to

D⁡(B𝐰​(n)​ℋ𝐰′​(n−2k))<D⁡(B𝐰​(n)​C𝐰​(n)​𝒢~𝐰′​(n−2k)).D(B_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w^{\prime}}}(n-2^{k}))<D(B_{\mathbf{w}}(n)C_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w^{\prime}}}(n-2^{k})).

The remainder of the argument is similar to that before.

Parts (b) and (c) follow directly from the statement (ii), which ensures that there is no cancellation of terms of degree DnD_{n} after substituting wj↦tjw_{j}\mapsto t^{j}. ∎

As it turns out, there is a curious connection between the sequence of degrees DnD_{n} and sums of sums of digits. For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} we let

Sn=∑ℓ=0ns⁡(ℓ),S_{n}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{n}s(\ell),

where ss denotes the sum of binary digits of nn.

Corollary 4.9.

Let n∈ℕ≥2n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} be such that 2k<n≤2k+12^{k}<n\leq 2^{k+1}. Then

Dn=Sn−1+Sn−2+k−1.D_{n}=S_{n-1}+S_{n-2}+k-1.
Proof.

Put Dn′=Sn−1+Sn−2+k−1D_{n}^{\prime}=S_{n-1}+S_{n-2}+k-1 for 2k<n≤2k+12^{k}<n\leq 2^{k+1}. We have D2=D2′=0D_{2}=D_{2}^{\prime}=0 so it suffices to show that Dn′D_{n}^{\prime} satisfies the same recurrence relations as in Proposition 4.8(a).

We recall two identities satisfied by SnS_{n}. Using the symmetry

s⁡(ℓ)+s⁡(2k+1−1−ℓ)=k+1,0≤ℓ<2k+1,s(\ell)+s(2^{k+1}-1-\ell)=k+1,\qquad 0\leq\ell<2^{k+1},

for m<2k+1−1m<2^{k+1}-1, one obtains

(13) Sm=S2k+1−m−2+(k+1)​(m−2k+1).S_{m}=S_{2^{k+1}-m-2}+(k+1)(m-2^{k}+1).

Moreover, for m<2km<2^{k} we have

(14) S2k+m=S2k−1+∑ℓ=0ms⁡(2k+ℓ)=k​2k−1+(m+1)+Sm.S_{2^{k}+m}=S_{2^{k}-1}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{m}s(2^{k}+\ell)=k2^{k-1}+(m+1)+S_{m}.

Now, suppose that 2k<n≤3⋅2k−12^{k}<n\leq 3\cdot 2^{k-1}. Applying (13) to m=n−1,n−2m=n-1,n-2, we get

Dn′\displaystyle D_{n}^{\prime} =S2k+1−n−1+S2k+1−n+(k+1)​(2​n−2k+1−1)+k−1\displaystyle=S_{2^{k+1}-n-1}+S_{2^{k+1}-n}+(k+1)(2n-2^{k+1}-1)+k-1
=D2k+1−n+1′+(k+1)​(2​n−2k+1−1)+1.\displaystyle=D_{2^{k+1}-n+1}^{\prime}+(k+1)(2n-2^{k+1}-1)+1.

If 3⋅2k−1<n≤2k+13\cdot 2^{k-1}<n\leq 2^{k+1}, then (14) applied to m=n−2k−1,n−2k−2m=n-2^{k}-1,n-2^{k}-2, gives

Dn′=k​2k+2​n−2k+1−1+Sn−2k−1+Sn−2k−2+k−1=2​n+2k​(k−2)+Dn−2k′,D_{n}^{\prime}=k2^{k}+2n-2^{k+1}-1+S_{n-2^{k}-1}+S_{n-2^{k}-2}+k-1=2n+2^{k}(k-2)+D_{n-2^{k}}^{\prime},

which ends the proof. ∎

We do not know whether this identity is purely coincidental or has a deeper reason.

4.4. Factorization of ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t)

In the next theorem, we describe the general structure of the polynomials ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t). It turns out that after dividing ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) by the factors tt and t−2t-2 (with multiplicity), all coefficients of the remaining factor have a common sign.

Theorem 4.10.

For n∈ℕ≥2n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} we have

ℋ⁡(n,t)=σ⁡(n)​tβ⁡(n)​(2−t)n−2​ℋ^​(n,t),\mathcal{H}(n,t)=\sigma(n)t^{\beta(n)}(2-t)^{n-2}\hat{\mathcal{H}}(n,t),

where ℋ^​(n,t)∈ℤ​[t]\hat{\mathcal{H}}(n,t)\in\mathbb{Z}[t] is a monic polynomial with all coefficients positive, and σ⁡(n)∈{1,−1}\sigma(n)\in\{1,-1\}, β⁡(n)∈ℕ\beta(n)\in\mathbb{N} satisfy

σ⁡(2)\displaystyle\sigma(2) =−1,\displaystyle=-1,
σ⁡(n)\displaystyle\sigma(n) ={(−1)n​σ​(2k+1−n+1)if ​2k<n≤3⋅2k−1,σ⁡(n−2k)if ​3⋅2k−1<n≤2k+1,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}(-1)^{n}\sigma(2^{k+1}-n+1)&\text{if }2^{k}<n\leq 3\cdot 2^{k-1},\\ \sigma(n-2^{k})&\text{if }3\cdot 2^{k-1}<n\leq 2^{k+1},\end{cases}
β⁡(2)\displaystyle\beta(2) =0,\displaystyle=0,
β⁡(n)\displaystyle\beta(n) ={β⁡(2k+1−n+1)+k⁡(2​n−2k+1−1)if ​2k<n≤3⋅2k−1,β⁡(n−2k)+k​2kif ​3⋅2k−1<n≤2k+1,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\beta(2^{k+1}-n+1)+k(2n-2^{k+1}-1)&\text{if }2^{k}<n\leq 3\cdot 2^{k-1},\\ \beta(n-2^{k})+k2^{k}&\text{if }3\cdot 2^{k-1}<n\leq 2^{k+1},\end{cases}
Proof.

We prove by induction that for 2k<n≤2k+12^{k}<n\leq 2^{k+1} the following two statements hold:

  1. (i)

    for all l≥1l\geq 1 there is a factorization

    h⁡(n,t,tk+l2l−1)\displaystyle h\left(n,t,\frac{t^{k+l}}{2^{l-1}}\right) =σ⁡(n)​tβn​(2−t)n−2​h^l​(n,t),\displaystyle=\sigma(n)t^{\beta_{n}}(2-t)^{n-2}\hat{h}_{l}(n,t),
    g~​(n,t,tk+l2l−1)\displaystyle\widetilde{g}\left(n,t,\frac{t^{k+l}}{2^{l-1}}\right) =(−1)n+1​σ​(n)​tβn​(2−t)n−1​g^l​(n,t),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n+1}\sigma(n)t^{\beta_{n}}(2-t)^{n-1}\hat{g}_{l}(n,t),

    where h^l​(n,t),g^l​(n,t)∈ℚ⁡[t]\hat{h}_{l}(n,t),\hat{g}_{l}(n,t)\in\mathbb{Q}[t] have all coefficients non-negative;

  2. (ii)

    deg⁡h^l​(n,t)≥k\deg\hat{h}_{l}(n,t)\geq k.

Along the way, we will also obtain the relations for σ⁡(n)\sigma(n) and β⁡(n)\beta(n).

We are going to use the notation

rl​(t)=tl−1+2​tl−2+⋯+2l−2​t+2l−1=tl−2lt−2.r_{l}(t)=t^{l-1}+2t^{l-2}+\cdots+2^{l-2}t+2^{l-1}=\frac{t^{l}-2^{l}}{t-2}.

For n=2,3,4n=2,3,4 our claim holds because

h⁡(2,t,tl2l−1)\displaystyle h\left(2,t,\frac{t^{l}}{2^{l-1}}\right) =−1,\displaystyle=-1,

4.5. Sign behavior

We now take a closer look at the sequence of signs σ⁡(n)\sigma(n) introduced in Theorem 4.10. In particular, the proposition implies that Hankel determinants for the usual binary sum of digits are nonzero.

Corollary 4.11.

For all n∈ℕ≥2n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} the Hankel determinant ℋ⁡(n,1)\mathcal{H}(n,1) is nonzero and we have

sgn⁡ℋ⁡(n,1)=σ⁡(n).\operatorname{sgn}\mathcal{H}(n,1)=\sigma(n).

The signs satisfy another, arguably simpler set of recurrence relations, where for convenience we define σ⁡(1)=1\sigma(1)=1.

Proposition 4.12.

For all n∈ℕ+n\in\mathbb{N}_{+} we have

(16) σ⁡(4​n)\displaystyle\sigma(4n) =(−1)n​σ​(2​n),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n}\sigma(2n),
σ⁡(4​n+1)\displaystyle\sigma(4n+1) =(−1)n​σ​(2​n+1),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n}\sigma(2n+1),
σ⁡(4​n+2)\displaystyle\sigma(4n+2) =(−1)n+1​σ​(2​n+1),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n+1}\sigma(2n+1),
σ⁡(4​n+3)\displaystyle\sigma(4n+3) =−σ⁡(2​n+1).\displaystyle=-\sigma(2n+1).
Proof.

We use induction on nn. For n=1,2n=1,2 our claim holds, and thus let n≥3n\geq 3. The argument is similar for each relation, so we only prove the second one. If 2k<4​n+1≤3⋅2k−12^{k}<4n+1\leq 3\cdot 2^{k-1}, then by Theorem 4.10 and the inductive assumption, we get

σ⁡(4​n+1)=−σ⁡(2k+1−4​n)=(−1)n+1​σ​(2k−2​n)=(−1)n​σ​(2​n+1)\sigma(4n+1)=-\sigma(2^{k+1}-4n)=(-1)^{n+1}\sigma(2^{k}-2n)=(-1)^{n}\sigma(2n+1)

If 3⋅2k−1<4​n+1≤2k+13\cdot 2^{k-1}<4n+1\leq 2^{k+1}, then again

σ⁡(4​n+1)=σ⁡(4​n−2k+1)=(−1)n​σ​(2​n−2k−1+1)=(−1)n​σ​(2​n+1),\sigma(4n+1)=\sigma(4n-2^{k}+1)=(-1)^{n}\sigma(2n-2^{k-1}+1)=(-1)^{n}\sigma(2n+1),

as desired. ∎

We now show that the ordinary generating function of the sequence (σ⁡(n))n≥1(\sigma(n))_{n\geq 1} of signs of ℋ⁡(n,1)\mathcal{H}(n,1) is transcendental. In particular, this implies that this sequence is not periodic.

Theorem 4.13.

Let F⁡(x)=∑n=1∞σ⁡(n)​xnF(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sigma(n)x^{n}. The function F⁡(x)F(x) is transcendental over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x). In particular, the sequence (σ⁡(n))n≥1(\sigma(n))_{n\geq 1} is not periodic.

Proof.

It is clear that to show that the function F⁡(x)F(x) is transcendental it is enough to show that its odd part

C⁡(x)=∑n=0∞σ⁡(2​n+1)​xnC(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sigma(2n+1)x^{n}

is transcendental. We split the series according to the parity of nn:

C⁡(x)=∑n=0∞σ⁡(4​n+1)​x2​n+∑n=0∞σ⁡(4​n+3)​x2​n+1,C(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sigma(4n+1)\,x^{2n}+\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sigma(4n+3)\,x^{2n+1},

and using the relations σ⁡(4​n+1)=(−1)n​σ​(2​n+1)\sigma(4n+1)=(-1)^{n}\sigma(2n+1) and σ⁡(4​n+3)=−σ⁡(2​n+1)\sigma(4n+3)=-\sigma(2n+1), we obtain the functional relation

(17) C⁡(x)=∑n≥0(−1)n​σ​(2​n+1)​x2​n−x​∑n≥0σ⁡(2​n+1)​x2​n=C⁡(−x2)−x​C​(x2).C(x)=\sum_{n\geq 0}(-1)^{n}\sigma(2n+1)x^{2n}-x\sum_{n\geq 0}\sigma(2n+1)x^{2n}=C(-x^{2})-xC(x^{2}).

Next, in order to eliminate the part with C⁡(−x2)C(-x^{2}) from (17), we replace xx by −x-x and get the relation C⁡(−x)=C⁡(−x2)+x​C​(x2)C(-x)=C(-x^{2})+xC(x^{2}), or equivalently C⁡(−x2)=C⁡(−x)−x​C​(x2)C(-x^{2})=C(-x)-xC(x^{2}). Putting this expression into (17) leads us to the identity

C⁡(−x)=2​x​C​(x2)+C⁡(x),C(-x)=2xC(x^{2})+C(x),

which, after replacing xx by x2x^{2}, gives the relation

C⁡(−x2)=2​x2​C​(x4)+C⁡(x2).C(-x^{2})=2x^{2}C(x^{4})+C(x^{2}).

Finally, we put the obtained expression for C⁡(−x2)C(-x^{2}) into (17) and obtain the functional relation for C⁡(x)C(x) in the following form:

(18) C⁡(x)+(x−1)​C​(x2)−2​x2​C​(x4)=0.C(x)+(x-1)C(x^{2})-2x^{2}C(x^{4})=0.

Because C⁡(x)C(x) satisfies a Mahler-type functional equation, we know, from the theorem of Nishioka [14, Theorem 5.1.7], that CC is rational or transcendental over ℚ⁡(x)\mathbb{Q}(x). Thus, it is enough to check that CC cannot represent a rational function.

For the contrary, suppose C⁡(x)C(x) is a rational function and not identically zero. Then we can write

C⁡(x)=P⁡(x)Q⁡(x),C(x)=\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)},

where P,Q∈ℂ⁡[x]P,Q\in\mathbb{C}[x], Q≢0Q\not\equiv 0 and gcd⁡(P,Q)=1\gcd(P,Q)=1. Let

p=deg⁡P,q=deg⁡Q,p=\deg P,\qquad q=\deg Q,

and let aa and bb be the leading coefficients of PP and QQ respectively, i.e.,

P⁡(x)=a​xp+(lower degree terms),Q⁡(x)=b​xq+(lower degree terms),P(x)=ax^{p}+\text{(lower degree terms)},\quad Q(x)=bx^{q}+\text{(lower degree terms)},

with a,b≠0a,b\neq 0.

We put the rational expression for C⁡(x)C(x) into (18) and clear denominators to obtain the polynomial equality

P⁡(x)​Q​(x2)​Q​(x4)=(1−x)​Q​(x)​P​(x2)​Q​(x4)+2​x2​Q​(x)​Q​(x2)​P​(x4).P(x)Q(x^{2})Q(x^{4})=(1-x)Q(x)P(x^{2})Q(x^{4})+2x^{2}Q(x)Q(x^{2})P(x^{4}).

The degrees of the particular terms (from left to right) are

p+6​q,1+2​p+5​q,2+4​p+3​q.p+6q,\qquad 1+2p+5q,\qquad 2+4p+3q.

By comparing the degrees we see that the only possibility for this equality to hold is that 1+2​p+5​q>2+4​p+3​q1+2p+5q>2+4p+3q. Indeed, if 1+2​p+5​q<2+4​p+3​q1+2p+5q<2+4p+3q, then p+6​q=2+4​p+3​qp+6q=2+4p+3q and we get 3​(q−p)=23(q-p)=2, a contradiction. If 1+2​p+5​q=2+4​p+3​q1+2p+5q=2+4p+3q, then 2​(q−p)=12(q-p)=1, also a contradiction. We thus have 1+2​p+5​q>2+4​p+3​q1+2p+5q>2+4p+3q, and then we get p+6​q=1+2​p+5​qp+6q=1+2p+5q, which implies q=p+1q=p+1.

However, the leading coefficient in P⁡(x)​Q​(x2)​Q​(x4)P(x)Q(x^{2})Q(x^{4}) is a​b2ab^{2}, and the leading coefficient in (1−x)​Q​(x)​P​(x2)​Q​(x4)(1-x)Q(x)P(x^{2})Q(x^{4}) is −a​b2-ab^{2}, and since the common degree of these polynomials is bigger than the degree of 2​x2​Q​(x)​Q​(x2)​P​(x4)2x^{2}Q(x)Q(x^{2})P(x^{4}), we get that 2​a​b2=02ab^{2}=0, which is a contradiction. ∎

4.6. Divisibility properties

Another consequence of (the proof of) Theorem 4.2 is a simpler recurrence relation describing the parity of ℋ𝐰​(n)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) for integer weights. As a special case, we can deduce the periodicity of ℋ⁡(n,1)mod2\mathcal{H}(n,1)\bmod{2}. These are Hankel determinants, reduced modulo 22, for the Thue–Morse sequence (Tn)n≥0(T_{n})_{n\geq 0}, defined by T0=0,T2​n=Tn,T2​n+1=1−TnT_{0}=0,T_{2n}=T_{n},T_{2n+1}=1-T_{n}. A similar result has already been proved for another variant of this sequence, with T0=1T_{0}=1 [1, Proposition 2.2].

Corollary 4.14.

Assume that wj∈ℤw_{j}\in\mathbb{Z} for all j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N}. Let n∈ℕ+n\in\mathbb{N}_{+} and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} be such that 2k<n≤2k+12^{k}<n\leq 2^{k+1}. Then

[ℋ𝐰​(n)𝒢~𝐰​(n)]≡wk+1​[1wk01]​[ℋ𝐰​(2k+1−n+1)𝒢~𝐰​(2k+1−n+1)](mod2).\begin{bmatrix}\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\\ \widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\end{bmatrix}\equiv w_{k+1}\begin{bmatrix}1&w_{k}\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k+1}-n+1)\\ \widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(2^{k+1}-n+1)\end{bmatrix}\pmod{2}.

In particular, Hankel determinants for the Thue–Morse sequence satisfy

ℋ⁡(n,1)≡n+1(mod2).\mathcal{H}(n,1)\equiv n+1\pmod{2}.
Proof.

After reducing modulo 22, the last summand in (8) becomes

uk+1​[0110]⊗K2k.u_{k+1}\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}\otimes K_{2^{k}}.

The remaining calculations proceed exactly as in Theorem 4.2(a). By reducing the formula there modulo 22, we obtain the first part of our claim.

The second part follows quickly by observing that for weights equal to 11, the determinants 𝒢~𝐰​(n)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{w}}(n) are odd for all n∈ℕ+n\in\mathbb{N}_{+}. ∎

It is natural to ask whether the following more general property holds.

Question 4.15.

Let k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}_{+}. Is the sequence (ℋ⁡(n+1,1)mod2k)n≥0(\mathcal{H}(n+1,1)\bmod{2^{k}})_{n\geq 0} 22-automatic?

Experimental computations suggest that the answer is affirmative at least for k=2k=2 and k=3k=3, where the automata generating the considered sequences have 1212 and 8383 states, respectively. Moreover, all possible remainders 0,1,…,2k−10,1,\ldots,2^{k}-1 seem to appear with similar frequency.

On the other hand, it turns out that almost all determinants ℋ⁡(n,1)\mathcal{H}(n,1) vanish modulo any fixed odd number (in the sense of density). We note that this fact follows from the results of Section 5.

Corollary 4.16.

For any odd m∈ℕ+m\in\mathbb{N}_{+} the set

{n≥1:m∣ℋ(n,1)}\{n\geq 1:m\mid\mathcal{H}(n,1)\}

has density 11.

Proof.

Let dd be such that 2d≡1(modm)2^{d}\equiv 1\pmod{m}. Then by Theorem 5.5 the set {n≥1:(td−2d)∣ℋ(n,t)}\{n\geq 1:(t^{d}-2^{d})\mid\mathcal{H}(n,t)\} has density 11. The result follows after inserting t=1t=1. ∎

5. Vanishing and non-vanishing of ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t)

In this section, we focus on the determinants ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) viewed as polynomials in tt. In particular, we study their vanishing and non-vanishing, which is important for the applications of Hankel determinants, as discussed in Section 1.

From the results proved so far, we can gather some facts concerning the roots of ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) for n∈ℕ≥2n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}:

  • •

    ℋ⁡(n,0)=0=ℋ⁡(n,2)\mathcal{H}(n,0)=0=\mathcal{H}(n,2) for n≥3n\geq 3;

  • •

    ℋ⁡(nk,ζ)=0\mathcal{H}(n_{k},\zeta)=0 for any (k+1)(k+1)st root of unity ζ\zeta, except ζ=1\zeta=1 (Theorem 4.4);

  • •

    the roots of ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) are algebraic integers (Proposition 4.8);

  • •

    if ℋ⁡(n,t)=0\mathcal{H}(n,t)=0 for some t∈ℝ∖{0,2}t\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,2\}, then t<0t<0 (Theorem 4.10).

One may ask the following natural questions:

  1. (1)

    What algebraic integers can be roots of ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) for some nn?

  2. (2)

    If ℋ⁡(n,t0)=0\mathcal{H}(n,t_{0})=0 for some n≥2n\geq 2 and t0∈ℂt_{0}\in\mathbb{C}, do there exist infinitely many such nn?

  3. (3)

    If the above is true, what is the order of the counting function of the set {n≥2:ℋ⁡(n,t0)=0}\{n\geq 2:\mathcal{H}(n,t_{0})=0\}?

5.1. Behavior at doubled roots of unity

We begin by exhibiting another infinite family of roots of the polynomials ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t), that is, doubled roots of unity. Instead of relying on the recursive formulas in Theorem 4.2, we take a more direct approach and explicitly construct nonzero vectors lying in ker⁡H⁡(n,2​ζ)\ker H(n,2\zeta) for certain nn, where ζd=1\zeta^{d}=1.

To begin, we give a simple but useful formula for a sum involving S⁡(n,2​ζ)S(n,2\zeta).

Lemma 5.1.

Let d∈ℕ+d\in\mathbb{N}_{+} and ζd=1\zeta^{d}=1. Then for each i=0,1,…,2di=0,1,\ldots,2^{d} we have

∑j=02d−1−1(S⁡(i+2​j+1,2​ζ)−S⁡(i+2​j,2​ζ))=2d−1.\sum_{j=0}^{2^{d-1}-1}(S(i+2j+1,2\zeta)-S(i+2j,2\zeta))=2^{d-1}.
Proof.

If ii is even, then each summand equals 11. If ii is odd, say i=2​k+1i=2k+1, we rewrite the sum as

S⁡(2d+2​k,2​ζ)−S⁡(2​k+1,2​ζ)−∑j=12d−1−1(S⁡(2​k+2​j+1,2​ζ)−S⁡(2​k+2​j,2​ζ))=\displaystyle S(2^{d}+2k,2\zeta)-S(2k+1,2\zeta)-\sum_{j=1}^{2^{d-1}-1}(S(2k+2j+1,2\zeta)-S(2k+2j,2\zeta))=
(2​ζ)d−1−(2d−1−1)=2d−1,\displaystyle(2\zeta)^{d}-1-(2^{d-1}-1)=2^{d-1},

and the lemma is proved. ∎

We will also need the formula in Proposition 4.1, which in the polynomial case wj=tjw_{j}=t^{j} takes the form

(19) H⁡(2k​n,t)=Jn⊗H⁡(2k,t)+tk​H​(n,t)⊗J2k+tk​F​(n,t)⊗K2k,H(2^{k}n,t)=J_{n}\otimes H(2^{k},t)+t^{k}H(n,t)\otimes J_{2^{k}}+t^{k}F(n,t)\otimes K_{2^{k}},

where

F⁡(n,t):=G⁡(n,t)−Jn=[S⁡(i+j+1,t)−S⁡(i+j,t)−1]0≤i,j<n.F(n,t):=G(n,t)-J_{n}=[S(i+j+1,t)-S(i+j,t)-1]_{0\leq i,j<n}.

This is precisely the matrix F𝐰​(n)F_{\mathbf{w}}(n), as in Section 4 for the weights wj=tjw_{j}=t^{j}.

We now show how to construct vectors in ker⁡H⁡(2d​n,2​ζ)\ker H(2^{d}n,2\zeta) for a ddth root of unity ζ\zeta. When writing the product ⊗\otimes of vectors or subspaces, we identify the tensor and Kronecker product.

Lemma 5.2.

Let d,n∈ℕ+d,n\in\mathbb{N}_{+} and ζd=1\zeta^{d}=1. Then

ker⁡F⁡(n,2​ζ)⊗ker⁡H⁡(2d,2​ζ)⊂ker⁡H⁡(2d​n,2​ζ).\ker F(n,2\zeta)\otimes\ker H(2^{d},2\zeta)\subset\ker H(2^{d}n,2\zeta).
Proof.

For each fixed d≥2d\geq 2 consider the set of indices as in Theorem 5.4:

Ad:=ℕ+∩⋃l=d+1∞⋃s∈ℕs​ odd(2ls−zd,l−1,2ls+zd,l+1].A_{d}:=\mathbb{N}_{+}\cap\bigcup_{l=d+1}^{\infty}\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in\mathbb{N}\\ s\text{ odd}\end{subarray}}(2^{l}s-z_{d,l}-1,2^{l}s+z_{d,l}+1].

In the following theorem we bound from above the counting function of the complement of AdA_{d}. In particular, the set of nn such that H⁡(n,2​ζ)≠0H(n,2\zeta)\neq 0 turns out to have density 00.

Theorem 5.5.

For real x≥1x\geq 1 we have

#⁡{n≤x:H⁡(n,−2)≠0}≤3​log2​x.\#\{n\leq x:H(n,-2)\neq 0\}\leq 3\log_{2}x.

If d≥3d\geq 3 and ζd=1\zeta^{d}=1, then

#⁡{n≤x:H⁡(n,2​ζ)≠0}=O⁡(xδd),\#\{n\leq x:H(n,2\zeta)\neq 0\}=O(x^{\delta_{d}}),\vskip-3.0pt

where δd<1+log2⁡(1−2−d)<1\delta_{d}<1+\log_{2}(1-2^{-d})<1.

Proof.

The claim for t=−2t=-2 follows directly from the second part of Theorem 5.4, hence fix d≥3d\geq 3. Instead of AdA_{d}, we consider the simpler set

A~d:=⋃l=2​d∞⋃s∈ℕs​ odd(2ls−2l−d,2ls+2l−d],\widetilde{A}_{d}:=\bigcup_{l=2d}^{\infty}\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in\mathbb{N}\\ s\text{ odd}\end{subarray}}(2^{l}s-2^{l-d},2^{l}s+2^{l-d}],

For k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} let A~d,k:=A~d∩(0,2k]\widetilde{A}_{d,k}:=\widetilde{A}_{d}\cap(0,2^{k}]. For k≥3​dk\geq 3d we have

λ((2k−A~d,k−1)∩(2k−2k−d,2k])=λ(−A~d,k−1∩(−2k−d,0])=ak−d.\lambda((2^{k}-\widetilde{A}_{d,k-1})\cap(2^{k}-2^{k-d},2^{k}])=\lambda(-\widetilde{A}_{d,k-1}\cap(-2^{k-d},0])=a_{k-d}.

Hence, for k≥3​dk\geq 3d we have the recurrence relation

ak=2​ak−1+2k−d−ak−d.a_{k}=2a_{k-1}+2^{k-d}-a_{k-d}.

bk=2​bk−1−bk−d.b_{k}=2b_{k-1}-b_{k-d}.

Moreover, we have R<2−21−dR<2-2^{1-d}, since BB is increasing in the interval (2​(d−1)d,+∞)(\frac{2(d-1)}{d},+\infty) containing 2−21−d2-2^{1-d}, and B⁡(2−21−d)>0B(2-2^{1-d})>0. Letting δd=log2⁡R\delta_{d}=\log_{2}R, we get bk=O⁡(2k​δ)b_{k}=O(2^{k\delta}). To finish the proof, let 2k−1≤x<2k2^{k-1}\leq x<2^{k} so that k=log2⁡x+O⁡(1)k=\log_{2}x+O(1). Then

Remark 5.6.

Since δd<1\delta_{d}<1, the theorem implies in particular that the set of indices n≤xn\leq x for which H⁡(n,2​ζ)≠0H(n,2\zeta)\neq 0 has sublinear growth.

We implemented the recurrence from Proposition  in Mathematica [13] to test the vanishing pattern predicted by Theorem 5.4. In particular, for all 2≤n≤10002\leq n\leq 1000 and for primitive roots of unity ζ\zeta of orders d=2,3,4,5,7d=2,3,4,5,7, the set of indices such that ℋ⁡(n,2​ζ)=0\mathcal{H}(n,2\zeta)=0 is precisely Ad∩{1,…,1000}A_{d}\cap\{1,\ldots,1000\}. This suggests the following conjecture.

Conjecture 5.7.

Let d∈ℕ≥2d\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}, and let ζ\zeta be a primitive ddth root of unity. Then for every n∈ℕ≥2n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}, we have

ℋ⁡(n,2​ζ)=0\mathcal{H}(n,2\zeta)=0

if and only if n∈Adn\in A_{d}.

In particular, ℋ⁡(n,−2)=0\mathcal{H}(n,-2)=0 if and only if n≠nk−1,nk,nk+1n\neq n_{k}-1,n_{k},n_{k}+1.

The “hard part” of the conjecture is to prove that the determinants ℋ⁡(n,2​ζ)\mathcal{H}(n,2\zeta) do not vanish outside of AdA_{d}. This is already known in the special case nk=⌈2k+2/3⌉n_{k}=\lceil 2^{k+2}/3\rceil, where the formula from Theorem 4.4 shows that the only roots of ℋ⁡(nk,t)\mathcal{H}(n_{k},t) are 0,20,2 and (k+1)(k+1)st roots of unity. However, such explicit characterizations seem rare. We now illustrate a possible different approach, which does not rely on computing the determinants directly.

Lemma 5.8.

Let n∈ℕ+n\in\mathbb{N}_{+} and assume that 𝟏n\mathbf{1}_{n} is in the image of H𝐰​(n)H_{\mathbf{w}}(n). If 𝒢𝐰​(n)≠0\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\neq 0, then ℋ𝐰​(n)≠0\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)\neq 0.

Proof.

Letting InI_{n} denote the n×nn\times n identity matrix, we have

H𝐰​(n)​(X​Rn−In)=𝟏n​Rn−H𝐰​(n)=[Rn−R0Rn−R1Rn−Rn−1]=[1⋯⋯10⋱⋱⋱0⋯01]​G𝐰​(n),H_{\mathbf{w}}(n)(XR_{n}-I_{n})=\mathbf{1}_{n}R_{n}-H_{\mathbf{w}}(n)=\begin{bmatrix}R_{n}-R_{0}\\ R_{n}-R_{1}\\ \vdots\\ R_{n}-R_{n-1}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&\cdots&\cdots&1\\ 0&\ddots&&\vdots\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ 0&\cdots&0&1\end{bmatrix}G_{\mathbf{w}}(n),

From the proof, we can derive the relation

(−1)n−1​(Rn​X−1)​ℋ𝐰​(n)=𝒢𝐰​(n).(-1)^{n-1}(R_{n}X-1)\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{w}}(n)=\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{w}}(n).

Theorem 5.10.

Let d∈ℕ≥2d\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2} and let ζ\zeta be a primitive root of unity of order dd. Then for any q≥1,r∈{0,1,…,d−1}q\geq 1,r\in\{0,1,\ldots,d-1\}, and

n=2q​d+r+2(q−1)​d+r+⋯+2d+r+2r=2r​2(q+1)​d−12d−1,n=2^{qd+r}+2^{(q-1)d+r}+\cdots+2^{d+r}+2^{r}=2^{r}\frac{2^{(q+1)d}-1}{2^{d}-1},

First, note that the binary expansion of nn is (10d−1)k​10r(10^{d-1})^{k}10^{r}, which means that 𝒢⁡(n,2​ζ)≠0\mathcal{G}(n,2\zeta)\neq 0 by Corollary 3.10. By Lemma 5.8 it remains to show that 𝟏n\mathbf{1}_{n} lies in the image of H⁡(n,2​ζ)H(n,2\zeta).

as in the proof of Lemma 5.2. Further, for l=d+1,…,2​d−1l=d+1,\ldots,2d-1 we put

Vl=Vd⊗[102l−d−1],V_{l}=V_{d}\otimes\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0_{2^{l-d}-1}\end{bmatrix},

which is a valid choice thanks to the equality (19) applied to k=l−d,n=2dk=l-d,n=2^{d}. Finally, for l≥2​dl\geq 2d we let

Vl=(𝟏2d−1⊗[10])⊗Vl−d,V_{l}=\left(\mathbf{1}_{2^{d-1}}\otimes\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}\right)\otimes V_{l-d},

Writing l=q​d+rl=qd+r as in the statement, we thus get z⁡(Vl)=n−2l−1z(V_{l})=n-2^{l}-1. A similar computation as in the proof of Theorem 5.4 shows that

H⁡(2l+1,2​ζ)​([10]⊗Vl)=[11]⊗αl​𝟏2l+(2​ζ)l​[02​ζ−2]⊗K2l​Vl.H(2^{l+1},2\zeta)\left(\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}\otimes V_{l}\right)=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\otimes\alpha_{l}\mathbf{1}_{2^{l}}+(2\zeta)^{l}\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 2\zeta-2\end{bmatrix}\otimes K_{2^{l}}V_{l}.

But K2l​VlK_{2^{l}}V_{l} has z⁡(Vl)+1z(V_{l})+1 leading zeros so the top 2l+z⁡(Vl)+1=n2^{l}+z(V_{l})+1=n entries in the whole vector are αl\alpha_{l}. It follows that

H⁡(n,2​ζ)​[Vl𝟎n−2l]=αl​𝟏n,H(n,2\zeta)\begin{bmatrix}V_{l}\\ \mathbf{0}_{n-2^{l}}\end{bmatrix}=\alpha_{l}\mathbf{1}_{n},

as desired. ∎

5.2. Vanishing of ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) for t≠0,2​ζt\neq 0,2\zeta

For other algebraic numbers tt it seems much harder to describe the set of nn such that ℋ⁡(n,t)=0\mathcal{H}(n,t)=0. However, as shown in the following result and its corollary, once it is known that ℋ⁡(n,t)=0\mathcal{H}(n,t)=0 for some n≥2n\geq 2, it is possible to construct infinitely many such indices.

Theorem 5.11.

Let t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} be such that t≠0t\neq 0 and t/2t/2 is not a root of unity. Let p,q∈ℕ+p,q\in\mathbb{N}_{+} be such that p≥3p\geq 3 is odd and ℋ⁡(p,t)=ℋ⁡(q,t)=0\mathcal{H}(p,t)=\mathcal{H}(q,t)=0. Then

ℋ⁡(2m​(p−1)+q,t)=0,\mathcal{H}(2^{m}(p-1)+q,t)=0,

where m∈ℕ+m\in\mathbb{N}_{+} is such that 2m−1<q≤2m2^{m-1}<q\leq 2^{m}.

Proof.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} be such that p≤2np\leq 2^{n}. There exist nonzero column vectors U′∈ℂpU^{\prime}\in\mathbb{C}^{p} and W′∈ℂqW^{\prime}\in\mathbb{C}^{q} such that H⁡(p,t)​U′=0H(p,t)U^{\prime}=0 and H⁡(q,t)​W′=0H(q,t)W^{\prime}=0. We pad U′U^{\prime} and W′W^{\prime} with trailing zeros, obtaining U∈ℂ2nU\in\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}} and W∈ℂ2mW\in\mathbb{C}^{2^{m}}.

For a vector V∈ℂkV\in\mathbb{C}^{k} we will now write Σ​V=𝟏kT​V\Sigma V=\mathbf{1}_{k}^{T}V to denote the sum of its components. Let V∈ℂ2nV\in\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}} and X∈ℂ2mX\in\mathbb{C}^{2^{m}} be such that

(20) H⁡(2n,t)​U\displaystyle H(2^{n},t)U =tn​K2n​V,\displaystyle=t^{n}K_{2^{n}}V,
H⁡(2m,t)​W\displaystyle H(2^{m},t)W =tm​K2m​X,\displaystyle=t^{m}K_{2^{m}}X,
Σ​U\displaystyle\Sigma U =Σ​V,\displaystyle=\Sigma V,
Σ​W\displaystyle\Sigma W =Σ​X.\displaystyle=\Sigma X.

This is possible since the first row of the matrices KlK_{l} is zero and the remaining rows are linearly independent.

Our goal now is to construct two vectors Y,Z∈ℂ2m+nY,Z\in\mathbb{C}^{2^{m+n}} satisfying

(21) H⁡(2m+n,t)​Y=tm+n​K2m+n​Z,H(2^{m+n},t)Y=t^{m+n}K_{2^{m+n}}Z,

such that YY ends with and ZZ begins with sufficiently many zeros, so that after truncating we get a nonzero vector Y′∈ker⁡H⁡(2m​(p−1)+q,t)Y^{\prime}\in\operatorname{ker}H(2^{m}(p-1)+q,t). They will be of the form

Y\displaystyle Y =A⊗W+B⊗X,\displaystyle=A\otimes W+B\otimes X,
Z\displaystyle Z =C⊗W+D⊗X,\displaystyle=C\otimes W+D\otimes X,

for some A,B,C,D∈ℂ2nA,B,C,D\in\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}} satisfying

(22) A+B\displaystyle A+B =U,\displaystyle=U,
C+D\displaystyle C+D =V,\displaystyle=V,
Σ​B\displaystyle\Sigma B =0,\displaystyle=0,
F⁡(2n,t)​A\displaystyle F(2^{n},t)A =tn​L2n​C.\displaystyle=t^{n}L_{2^{n}}C.

We first choose AA so that it ends with many zeros, CC resulting from (22) begins with many zeros, and Σ​A=Σ​U\Sigma A=\Sigma U. We claim that it is possible to choose a vector A′A^{\prime} (which will constitute the first pp components of AA) from the kernel of F⁡(p,t)F(p,t), in such a way that Σ​A′=Σ​U\Sigma A^{\prime}=\Sigma U. If Σ​U=0\Sigma U=0, we simply take A′=𝟎pA^{\prime}=\mathbf{0}_{p}. Otherwise, if Σ​U≠0\Sigma U\neq 0, we use the fact that the matrix F⁡(p,t)F(p,t) is singular for pp odd. Suppose by contradiction that Σ​A′=0\Sigma A^{\prime}=0 for all A′∈ker⁡F⁡(p,t)A^{\prime}\in\operatorname{ker}F(p,t). Because the matrix F⁡(p,t)F(p,t) is symmetric, 𝟏p\mathbf{1}_{p} must lie in its image, and thus Jp=F⁡(p,t)​QJ_{p}=F(p,t)Q for a p×pp\times p matrix QQ. Consequently, the matrix G⁡(p,t)=F⁡(p,t)+JpG(p,t)=F(p,t)+J_{p} is also singular. But this cannot be the case, as by Corollary 3.10 the roots of 𝒢⁡(p,t)\mathcal{G}(p,t) are t=0t=0 and t=2​ζt=2\zeta, where ζ\zeta is a root of unity. Hence, there exists A′∈ker⁡F⁡(p,t)A^{\prime}\in\operatorname{ker}F(p,t) wih Σ​A′\Sigma A^{\prime} nonzero and after scaling we can assume Σ​A′=Σ​U\Sigma A^{\prime}=\Sigma U. Then A∈ℂ2nA\in\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}} is obtained by padding A′A^{\prime} with 2n−p2^{n}-p trailing zeros, so that Σ​A=Σ​U\Sigma A=\Sigma U holds. The remaining vectors B,C,DB,C,D are uniquely determined by the imposed conditions (22).

Next, we show that the relations (20) and (22) imply equality (21). We expand H⁡(2m+n,t)​YH(2^{m+n},t)Y using Proposition 4.1, obtaining three products on the left-hand side. The first is

(J2n⊗H⁡(2m,t))​Y\displaystyle(J_{2^{n}}\otimes H(2^{m},t))Y =J2n​A⊗H⁡(2m,t)​W+J2n​B⊗H⁡(2m,t)​X\displaystyle=J_{2^{n}}A\otimes H(2^{m},t)W+J_{2^{n}}B\otimes H(2^{m},t)X
=tm​(Σ​U)​𝟏2n⊗K2m​X.\displaystyle=t^{m}(\Sigma U)\mathbf{1}_{2^{n}}\otimes K_{2^{m}}X.

The second product is

(tm​H​(2n,t)⊗J2m)​Y\displaystyle(t^{m}H(2^{n},t)\otimes J_{2^{m}})Y =tm​H​(2n,t)​A⊗J2m​W+tm​H​(2n,t)​B⊗J2m​X\displaystyle=t^{m}H(2^{n},t)A\otimes J_{2^{m}}W+t^{m}H(2^{n},t)B\otimes J_{2^{m}}X
=tm+n​(Σ​W)​K2n​V⊗𝟏2m.\displaystyle=t^{m+n}(\Sigma W)K_{2^{n}}V\otimes\mathbf{1}_{2^{m}}.

The final product on the left-hand side is

OPENtm​(F⁡(2n,t)⊗K2m))​Y\displaystyle t^{m}(F(2^{n},t)\otimes K_{2^{m}}))Y =tm​F​(2n,t)​A⊗K2m​W+tm​F​(2n,t)​B⊗K2m​X\displaystyle=t^{m}F(2^{n},t)A\otimes K_{2^{m}}W+t^{m}F(2^{n},t)B\otimes K_{2^{m}}X
=tm+n​L2n​C⊗K2m​W+tm​F​(2n,t)​B⊗K2m​X\displaystyle=t^{m+n}L_{2^{n}}C\otimes K_{2^{m}}W+t^{m}F(2^{n},t)B\otimes K_{2^{m}}X

The right-hand side of (21) is

tm+n​(L2n⊗K2m+K2n⊗J2m)​Z=\displaystyle t^{m+n}\bigl(L_{2^{n}}\otimes K_{2^{m}}+K_{2^{n}}\otimes J_{2^{m}}\bigr)Z=
tm+n​(L2n​C⊗K2m​W+L2n​D⊗K2m​X+(Σ​W)​K2n​V⊗𝟏2m).\displaystyle t^{m+n}\bigl(L_{2^{n}}C\otimes K_{2^{m}}W+L_{2^{n}}D\otimes K_{2^{m}}X+(\Sigma W)K_{2^{n}}V\otimes\mathbf{1}_{2^{m}}\bigr).

In order to prove our claim it remains to show that

F⁡(2n,t)​B+𝟏2n=tn​L2n​D.F(2^{n},t)B+\mathbf{1}_{2^{n}}=t^{n}L_{2^{n}}D.

After adding F⁡(2n,t)​A=tn​L2n​CF(2^{n},t)A=t^{n}L_{2^{n}}C to both sides and multiplying by L2nL_{2^{n}} from the left, this is equivalent to

(23) tn​V=L2n​F​(2n,t)​U+(Σ​U)​𝟏2n.t^{n}V=L_{2^{n}}F(2^{n},t)U+(\Sigma U)\mathbf{1}_{2^{n}}.

Note that, given UU, the conditions H⁡(2n,t)​U=tn​K2n​VH(2^{n},t)U=t^{n}K_{2^{n}}V and Σ​U=Σ​V\Sigma U=\Sigma V determine VV uniquely. Hence, it is enough to check that VV as in (23) satisfies them both. The first one follows from the identity

H⁡(2n,t)=K2n​(L2n​F​(2n,t)+J2n)+𝟏2n​[S⁡(0,t)⋯S⁡(2n−1,t)],H(2^{n},t)=K_{2^{n}}(L_{2^{n}}F(2^{n},t)+J_{2^{n}})+\mathbf{1}_{2^{n}}\begin{bmatrix}S(0,t)&\cdots&S(2^{n}-1,t)\end{bmatrix},

which in turn is a direct consequence of the definition of FF. The second condition is obtained by summing the components of both sides of (23) and using the equality

𝟏2nT​F​(2n,t)=(tn−2n)​𝟏2nT.\mathbf{1}_{2^{n}}^{T}F(2^{n},t)=(t^{n}-2^{n})\mathbf{1}_{2^{n}}^{T}.

We now count the trailing zeros in YY and the leading zeros in ZZ, where the given amounts are not necessarily maximal. Both AA and UU end with 2n−p2^{n}-p zeros, hence so does B=U−AB=U-A. It follows that YY ends with 2n−p2^{n}-p blocks of zeros having length 2m2^{m}. Additionally, the (p−1)(p-1)st block in YY (numbering from 00) is a linear combination of WW and XX, and these vectors end with 2m−q2^{m}-q and q−1q-1 zeros, respectively. Since q−1>2m−qq-1>2^{m}-q, we deduce that YY ends with 2m​(2n−p)+2m−q=2m+n−(2m​(p−1)+q)2^{m}(2^{n}-p)+2^{m}-q=2^{m+n}-(2^{m}(p-1)+q) zeros. Furthermore, from the relations F⁡(p,t)​A′=𝟎pF(p,t)A^{\prime}=\mathbf{0}_{p} and F⁡(2n,t)​A=tn​L2n​CF(2^{n},t)A=t^{n}L_{2^{n}}C we deduce that CC ends with pp zeros. At the same time, VV ends with p−1p-1 zeros, which means that D=V−CD=V-C also ends with p−1p-1 zeros. Hence, ZZ ends with p−1p-1 blocks of zeros of length 2m2^{m} and the previous block is a multiple of XX. Therefore, ZZ ends with at least 2m​(p−1)+q−12^{m}(p-1)+q-1 zeros. If we let Y′Y^{\prime} denote the vector YY truncated to the initial 2m​(p−1)+q2^{m}(p-1)+q components, then by the above considerations (21) implies

H⁡(2m​(p−1)+q,t)​Y′=𝟎2m​(p−1)+q.H(2^{m}(p-1)+q,t)Y^{\prime}=\mathbf{0}_{2^{m}(p-1)+q}.

It remains to show that Y′Y^{\prime}, or equivalently, YY is nonzero. Suppose by contradiction that Y=A⊗W+B⊗XY=A\otimes W+B\otimes X is the zero vector.

Since A+B=U≠𝟎2nA+B=U\neq\mathbf{0}_{2^{n}}, at least one of A,BA,B is non-zero, and thus X,WX,W must be linearly dependent. Because WW is non-zero, we can write X=α​WX=\alpha W for some α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}, which gives Y=(A+α​B)⊗WY=(A+\alpha B)\otimes W, and consequently A+α​B=𝟎2nA+\alpha B=\mathbf{0}_{2^{n}}. Then Σ​U=0\Sigma U=0, in which case we have chosen A=𝟎2nA=\mathbf{0}_{2^{n}} in an earlier step in the proof. It follows that α=0\alpha=0, meaning that X=𝟎2mX=\mathbf{0}_{2^{m}}. By the conditions (20), we have H⁡(2m,t)​W=𝟎2mH(2^{m},t)W=\mathbf{0}_{2^{m}} and Σ​W=Σ​X=0\Sigma W=\Sigma X=0. Since the matrix H⁡(2m,t)H(2^{m},t) is symmetric, 𝟏2m\mathbf{1}_{2^{m}} belongs to its image. But 𝒢⁡(n,t)≠0\mathcal{G}(n,t)\neq 0 by Corollary 3.10 so Lemma 5.8 implies H⁡(2m,t)H(2^{m},t) is non-singular, a contradiction. ∎

If we take q=pq=p in the theorem, we can construct a sequence of indices such that ℋ⁡(pk,t)=0\mathcal{H}(p_{k},t)=0.

Corollary 5.12.

Let t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} be such that t≠0t\neq 0 and t/2t/2 is not a root of unity. Let p≥3p\geq 3 be odd and such that ℋ⁡(p,t)=0\mathcal{H}(p,t)=0. Then for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} we have

ℋ⁡(pk,t)=0,\mathcal{H}(p_{k},t)=0,

where

pk=(p−1)​2(k+1)​m−12m−1+1p_{k}=(p-1)\frac{2^{(k+1)m}-1}{2^{m}-1}+1

and m∈ℕ+m\in\mathbb{N}_{+} is such that 2m−1<p≤2m2^{m-1}<p\leq 2^{m}.

Proof.

By Theorem 5.11 we have ℋ⁡(pk′,t)=0\mathcal{H}(p^{\prime}_{k},t)=0, where p0′=pp^{\prime}_{0}=p and pk+1′=2m​(pk′−1)+pp^{\prime}_{k+1}=2^{m}(p^{\prime}_{k}-1)+p. It is easy to check by induction that pk′=pkp^{\prime}_{k}=p_{k}. ∎

For example, if we take t=−1t=-1 and p=3,2m=4p=3,2^{m}=4, then we retrieve the subsequence pk=n2​k+1p_{k}=n_{2k+1}, where nkn_{k} is defined by (9).

6. Further questions and problems

We conclude with several additional questions and problems that are naturally suggested by the results of this paper.

Problem 6.1.

Let t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} be fixed and such that ℋ⁡(n,t)=0\mathcal{H}(n,t)=0 for some n∈ℕ≥2n\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2}. Describe the structure of the set

{n≥0:ℋ⁡(n,t)=0}.\{n\geq 0:\mathcal{H}(n,t)=0\}.

In particular, is this set automatic?

In view of the polynomial formula in Theorem 4.4 and the vanishing patterns obtained in Section 5, this is an interesting question especially in the case when t=ζt=\zeta and t=2​ζt=2\zeta, where ζ\zeta is a root of unity.

Question 6.2.

Do there exist n≥2n\geq 2 and t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} such that ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) has a multiple root at tt, other than t=0t=0 and t=2​ζt=2\zeta?

Another interesting problem is further restricting the set of possible roots of the polynomials (ℋ⁡(n,t))n≥2(\mathcal{H}(n,t))_{n\geq 2}. We state two further questions in this direction.

Question 6.3.

Does there exist a uniform bound |t|≤M|t|\leq M satisfied by all roots of ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) for all n≥2n\geq 2?

Experimental computations suggest that the answer is affirmative and the optimal bound is M=5+32M=\frac{\sqrt{5}+3}{2}. Moreover, the value −5+32-\frac{\sqrt{5}+3}{2} can apparently be approached from above by real roots of the polynomials ℋ⁡(ak,t)\mathcal{H}(a_{k},t), where a0=5a_{0}=5 and

ak+1={2​akif ​k≡0,1(mod4),2​ak−1if ​k≡2,3(mod4).a_{k+1}=\begin{cases}2a_{k}&\text{if }k\equiv 0,1\pmod{4},\\ 2a_{k}-1&\text{if }k\equiv 2,3\pmod{4}.\end{cases}
Question 6.4.

Is it true that for every fixed degree D≥1D\geq 1 there exist only finitely many algebraic numbers t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C} of degree at most DD such that ℋ⁡(n,t)=0\mathcal{H}(n,t)=0 for some n≥2n\geq 2?

Equivalently, do the polynomials ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) have only finitely many distinct irreducible factors of any fixed degree over ℚ\mathbb{Q}? Our computations suggest that this is indeed the case.

Problem 6.5.

Find further natural families of indices nn for which ℋ⁡(n,t)\mathcal{H}(n,t) admits a simple closed formula (for general tt as well as for fixed OPENt=t0)t=t_{0}).

Besides Theorem 4.4, the formulas from Proposition 4.5 suggest that other such families may exist.

Problem 6.6.

Describe more precisely the set of non-vanishing indices for t=2​ζt=2\zeta, where ζ\zeta is a root of unity.

Theorems 5.4 and 5.5 show that this set is sparse, but its finer structure remains unclear.

A natural direction of further research is to consider more general sequences than those considered in the paper. In particular, the methods of the paper are strongly tied to the binary expansion, but it is natural to ask to what extent they persist in other bases. More precisely, we formulate the following problem.

Problem 6.7.

Extend the results of this paper to weighted sum-of-digits functions in base b≥2b\geq 2.

One may also ask for the values of Hankel determinants for a shift of the sequence (s𝐰​(n))n≥0(s_{\mathbf{w}}(n))_{n\geq 0}, as was done in [1] in the Thue–Morse case.

Problem 6.8.

Find recursive or explicit formulas for Hankel determinants corresponding to the shifted sequence (s𝐰​(n+k))n≥0(s_{\mathbf{w}}(n+k))_{n\geq 0}, where k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}.

Finally, we formulate the following general problem.

Problem 6.9.

Investigate Hankel determinants associated with other regular digital sequences, for instance sequences counting occurrences of a fixed block in the base-bb expansion of nn.

These sequences share many structural features with weighted sum-of-digits functions and may exhibit similar determinant phenomena.
